(iii) 3x - 2y >= 6: Associated equation 3x - 2y = 6; intercepts (2, 0) and (0, -3); solid line. Test (0, 0): 0 >= 6 is false. Shade the half-plane below-right of the line, away from the origin, including the line.

(iv) 5x - 4y <= 20: Associated equation 5x - 4y = 20; intercepts (4, 0) and (0, -5); solid line. Test (0, 0): 0 <= 20 is true. Shade the half-plane above-left of the line, the side containing the origin, including the line.

(v) 2x + 1 >= 0, i.e. x >= -1/2: Associated equation x = -1/2, a vertical solid line through (-1/2, 0). Shade the closed half-plane to the RIGHT of this line.

(vi) 3y - 4 <= 0, i.e. y <= 4/3: Associated equation y = 4/3, a horizontal solid line through (0, 4/3). Shade the closed half-plane BELOW this line.

Q4: Indicate the solution region of the following linear inequalities by shading

(i) 2x - 3y <= 6 ; 2x + 3y <= 12 (ii) x + y >= 5 ; -y + x <= 1 (iii) 3x + 7y >= 21 ; x - y <= 2 (iv) 4x - 3y <= 12 ; x >= -3/2 (v) 3x + 7y >= 21 ; y <= 4 (vi) 5x + 7y <= 35 ; x - 2y <= 2

Procedure: Graph each inequality as in Q.3 on the same axes; the solution region is the part common to all of them. Corner points are found by solving the two associated equations simultaneously. [All six graphs are described in words — see manifest flag.]

(i) 2x - 3y <= 6 and 2x + 3y <= 12: Line 1 (2x - 3y = 6) passes through (3, 0) and (0, -2); test (0, 0): 0 <= 6 true, take the origin side (above the line). Line 2 (2x + 3y = 12) passes through (6, 0) and (0, 4); test (0, 0): 0 <= 12 true, take the origin side (below the line). The common region is an unbounded wedge containing the origin, with the single corner where the lines cross: adding the equations, 4x = 18, so x = 9/2; then 9 - 3y = 6 gives y = 1. Corner point: (9/2, 1).

(ii) x + y >= 5 and x - y <= 1: Line 1 (x + y = 5) through (5, 0), (0, 5); test (0, 0): 0 >= 5 false, take the side away from the origin. Line 2 (x - y = 1) through (1, 0), (0, -1); test (0, 0): 0 <= 1 true, take the origin side. Common region: unbounded, with corner where x + y = 5 and x - y = 1 meet: adding, 2x = 6, x = 3; then y = 2. Corner point: (3, 2).

(iii) 3x + 7y >= 21 and x - y <= 2: Line 1 through (7, 0), (0, 3); take the side away from the origin. Line 2 (x - y = 2) through (2, 0), (0, -2); take the origin side. Corner: from line 2, x = y + 2; substitute in line 1: 3(y + 2) + 7y = 21, so 10y = 15, y = 3/2, x = 7/2. Corner point: (7/2, 3/2). Region unbounded.

(iv) 4x - 3y <= 12 and x >= -3/2: Line 1 (4x - 3y = 12) through (3, 0), (0, -4); take the origin side. Line 2 is the vertical line x = -3/2; take the right side. Corner: put x = -3/2 in line 1: -6 - 3y = 12, so y = -6. Corner point: (-3/2, -6). Region unbounded.

(v) 3x + 7y >= 21 and y <= 4: Line 1 through (7, 0), (0, 3); take the side away from the origin. Line 2 is the horizontal line y = 4; take the side below it. Corner: put y = 4 in line 1: 3x + 28 = 21, so x = -7/3. Corner point: (-7/3, 4). Region unbounded.

(vi) 5x + 7y <= 35 and x - 2y <= 2: Line 1 (5x + 7y = 35) through (7, 0), (0, 5); take the origin side (below the line). Line 2 (x - 2y = 2) through (2, 0), (0, -1); test (0, 0): 0 <= 2 true, take the origin side (above the line). Common region: an unbounded wedge containing the origin, with corner where the lines cross: from line 2, x = 2 + 2y; substitute: 5(2 + 2y) + 7y = 35, so 17y = 25, y = 25/17, x = 84/17. Corner point: (84/17, 25/17).

mcqs.q: The solution of 12x + 30 = -6 is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Subtract 30 from both sides: 12x = -6 - 30 = -36. Step 2: Divide both sides by 12: x = -36/12 = -3. On the real line it is shown by a filled dot at -3.

mcqs.q: The solution of x/3 + 6 = -12 is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Subtract 6 from both sides: x/3 = -12 - 6 = -18. Step 2: Multiply both sides by 3: x = -54.

mcqs.q: The solution of x/2 - 3x/4 = 1/12 is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: With LCM 4: (2x - 3x)/4 = 1/12, so -x/4 = 1/12. Step 2: Multiply both sides by -4: x = -4/12 = -1/3.

mcqs.q: The solution of 2 = 7(2x + 4) + 12x is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Expand: 2 = 14x + 28 + 12x = 26x + 28. Step 2: Subtract 28: -26 = 26x. Step 3: x = -26/26 = -1.

mcqs.q: The solution of the inequality x - 6 <= -2 is:
mcqs.why: Step: Add 6 to both sides (inequality unchanged): x <= -2 + 6 = 4. The endpoint 4 is included, so on the real line it is a filled circle at 4 with the arrow to the left.

mcqs.q: The solution of the inequality -9 > -16 + x is:
mcqs.why: Step: Add 16 to both sides: -9 + 16 > x, i.e. 7 > x, which is x < 7. The endpoint 7 is excluded, shown by an open circle at 7 with the arrow to the left.

mcqs.q: The solution of the inequality 6(x + 10) <= 0 is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Divide both sides by 6 (positive, so the sign stays): x + 10 <= 0. Step 2: Subtract 10: x <= -10.

mcqs.q: When both sides of an inequality are multiplied or divided by a NEGATIVE number:
options: the inequality sign stays the same
mcqs.why: Rule: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the direction of the inequality. For example, -(1/4)x <= -1/2 multiplied by -4 gives x >= 2, not x <= 2.

mcqs.q: For the inequality 2x + y <= 6, the boundary line is drawn SOLID and the origin side is shaded because:
options: the line must always be solid for every inequality
(0, 0) does not satisfy it: 0 <= 6 is false
the inequality includes equality (<=) and (0, 0) satisfies it: 0 <= 6 is true
mcqs.why: The line is solid when the inequality is <= or >= (points on the line are included). Testing (0, 0): 2(0) + 0 = 0 <= 6 is true, so the half-plane containing the origin is shaded. The intercepts (3, 0) and (0, 6) are used to draw the line, but they do not decide the shading.

mcqs.q: The corner point of the common solution region of 2x - 3y <= 6 and 2x + 3y <= 12 is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Solve the associated equations together: adding 2x - 3y = 6 and 2x + 3y = 12 gives 4x = 18, so x = 9/2. Step 2: Substitute in 2x - 3y = 6: 9 - 3y = 6, so y = 1. Corner point: (9/2, 1).

lessons.title: Exercise 5.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: Maximize f(x, y) = 2x + 5y; subject to the constraints 2y - x <= 8 ; x - y <= 4 ; x >= 0 ; y >= 0

Maximize f(x, y) = 2x + 5y.

Procedure: (1) Draw the feasible region from the constraints. (2) Find its corner points (axes intercepts and intersections of boundary lines). (3) Evaluate the objective function at every corner point; the largest value is the maximum.

Step 1: Constraints: 2y - x <= 8 gives y <= (x + 8)/2 (line through (0, 4) and (-8, 0)); x - y <= 4 gives y >= x - 4 (line through (4, 0) and (0, -4)); with x >= 0, y >= 0 the region is bounded.

Step 2: Corner points: (0, 0); on the y-axis from 2y <= 8: (0, 4); on the x-axis from x <= 4: (4, 0); intersection of the two lines: 2y = x + 8 and y = x - 4 gives 2(x - 4) = x + 8, so x = 16, y = 12: point (16, 12).

Step 3: Evaluate f(x, y) = 2x + 5y: f(0, 0) = 0; f(0, 4) = 20; f(4, 0) = 8; f(16, 12) = 32 + 60 = 92.

Hence the maximum value of f is 92 at the corner point (16, 12).

Q2: Maximize f(x, y) = x + 3y; subject to the constraints 2x + 5y <= 30 ; 5x + 4y <= 20 ; x >= 0 ; y >= 0

Maximize f(x, y) = x + 3y.

Step 1: Boundary lines: 2x + 5y = 30 (intercepts (15, 0), (0, 6)) and 5x + 4y = 20 (intercepts (4, 0), (0, 5)). The feasible region lies below both lines in the first quadrant.

Step 2: The two lines cross where 2x + 5y = 30 and 5x + 4y = 20: multiplying the first by 5 and the second by 2 and subtracting gives 17y = 110, y = 110/17, which makes x negative — outside the first quadrant. So the binding boundary is 5x + 4y = 20 only, and the corner points are (0, 0), (4, 0) and (0, 5). (Check (0, 5) in the first constraint: 25 <= 30 ✓; (4, 0): 8 <= 30 ✓.)

Step 3: Evaluate f(x, y) = x + 3y: f(0, 0) = 0; f(4, 0) = 4; f(0, 5) = 15.

Hence the maximum value of f is 15 at the corner point (0, 5).

Q3: Maximize z = 2x + 3y; subject to the constraints 2x + y <= 4 ; 4x - y <= 2 ; x >= 0 ; y >= 0

Maximize z = 2x + 3y.

Step 1: Boundary lines: 2x + y = 4 (intercepts (2, 0), (0, 4)) and 4x - y = 2 (intercepts (1/2, 0), (0, -2)). Feasible region in the first quadrant below line 1 and above line 2 (origin side).

Step 2: Corner points: (0, 0); (1/2, 0) (from 4x <= 2 on the x-axis); (0, 4) (from y <= 4 on the y-axis); intersection of the lines: adding 2x + y = 4 and 4x - y = 2 gives 6x = 6, so x = 1, y = 2: point (1, 2).

Step 3: Evaluate z = 2x + 3y: z(0, 0) = 0; z(1/2, 0) = 1; z(0, 4) = 12; z(1, 2) = 2 + 6 = 8.

Hence the maximum value of z is 12 at the corner point (0, 4).

Q4: Minimize z = 2x + y; subject to the constraints x + y >= 3 ; 7x + 5y <= 35 ; x >= 0 ; y >= 0

Minimize z = 2x + y.

Step 1: Feasible region: above the line x + y = 3, below the line 7x + 5y = 35, in the first quadrant.

Step 2: Corner points: (0, 3) (y-intercept of x + y = 3; check 5(3) = 15 <= 35 ✓); (3, 0) (x-intercept of x + y = 3; check 21 <= 35 ✓); (5, 0) (x-intercept of 7x + 5y = 35); (0, 7) (y-intercept of 7x + 5y = 35). (The two lines cross at (10, -7), outside the first quadrant, so it is not a corner of the feasible region.)

Step 3: Evaluate z = 2x + y: z(0, 3) = 3; z(3, 0) = 6; z(5, 0) = 10; z(0, 7) = 7.

Hence the minimum value of z is 3 at the corner point (0, 3).

Q5: Maximize the function f(x, y) = 2x + 3y subject to the constraints 2x + y <= 10 ; x + 2y <= 14 ; x >= 0 ; y >= 0

Maximize f(x, y) = 2x + 3y.

Step 1: Boundary lines: 2x + y = 10 (intercepts (5, 0), (0, 10)) and x + 2y = 14 (intercepts (14, 0), (0, 7)). Feasible region below both lines in the first quadrant.

Step 2: Corner points: (0, 0); (5, 0); (0, 7); intersection: from 2x + y = 10, y = 10 - 2x; substitute in x + 2y = 14: x + 20 - 4x = 14, so -3x = -6, x = 2, y = 6: point (2, 6).

Step 3: Evaluate f(x, y) = 2x + 3y: f(0, 0) = 0; f(5, 0) = 10; f(0, 7) = 21; f(2, 6) = 4 + 18 = 22.

Hence the maximum value of f is 22 at the corner point (2, 6).

Q6: Find minimum and maximum values of z = 3x + y; subject to the constraints 3x + 5y >= 15 ; x + 3y <= 9 ; x >= 0 ; y >= 0

Find the minimum and maximum values of z.

Step 1: Feasible region: above the line 3x + 5y = 15 (intercepts (5, 0), (0, 3)) and below the line x + 3y = 9 (intercepts (9, 0), (0, 3)), in the first quadrant.

Step 2: The two lines meet where 3x + 5y = 15 and x + 3y = 9: from the second, x = 9 - 3y; substitute: 3(9 - 3y) + 5y = 15, so 27 - 4y = 15, y = 3, x = 0: point (0, 3) — both lines pass through (0, 3). Corner points of the triangular region: (0, 3), (5, 0), (9, 0).

Step 3: Evaluate z = 3x + y: z(0, 3) = 3; z(5, 0) = 15; z(9, 0) = 27.

Hence the minimum value of z is 3 at (0, 3) and the maximum value of z is 27 at (9, 0).

mcqs.q: Maximize f(x, y) = 2x + 5y subject to 2y - x <= 8, x - y <= 4, x >= 0, y >= 0. The maximum value is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Corner points of the feasible region: (0, 0), (0, 4), (4, 0) and the intersection (16, 12) of the two boundary lines. Step 2: f(0, 0) = 0, f(0, 4) = 20, f(4, 0) = 8, f(16, 12) = 2(16) + 5(12) = 32 + 60 = 92. The largest value is 92 at (16, 12).

mcqs.q: Maximize f(x, y) = x + 3y subject to 2x + 5y <= 30, 5x + 4y <= 20, x >= 0, y >= 0. The maximum value is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: The corner points are (0, 0), (4, 0) and (0, 5) — the two lines cross outside the first quadrant, so only 5x + 4y = 20 binds. Step 2: f(0, 0) = 0, f(4, 0) = 4, f(0, 5) = 15. The maximum is 15 at (0, 5).

mcqs.q: Maximize z = 2x + 3y subject to 2x + y <= 4, 4x - y <= 2, x >= 0, y >= 0. The maximum value is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Corner points: (0, 0), (1/2, 0), (0, 4) and (1, 2) (intersection of the lines). Step 2: z(0, 0) = 0, z(1/2, 0) = 1, z(0, 4) = 12, z(1, 2) = 8. The maximum is 12 at (0, 4).

mcqs.q: Minimize z = 2x + y subject to x + y >= 3, 7x + 5y <= 35, x >= 0, y >= 0. The minimum value is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Corner points: (0, 3), (3, 0), (5, 0) and (0, 7). Step 2: z(0, 3) = 3, z(3, 0) = 6, z(5, 0) = 10, z(0, 7) = 7. The smallest value is 3 at (0, 3).

mcqs.q: Maximize f(x, y) = 2x + 3y subject to 2x + y <= 10, x + 2y <= 14, x >= 0, y >= 0. The maximum value is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Corner points: (0, 0), (5, 0), (0, 7) and the intersection (2, 6) of 2x + y = 10 and x + 2y = 14. Step 2: f(0, 0) = 0, f(5, 0) = 10, f(0, 7) = 21, f(2, 6) = 4 + 18 = 22. The maximum is 22 at (2, 6).

mcqs.q: For z = 3x + y subject to 3x + 5y >= 15, x + 3y <= 9, x >= 0, y >= 0, the minimum and maximum values are:
mcqs.why: Step 1: The triangular feasible region has corners (0, 3), (5, 0) and (9, 0). Step 2: z(0, 3) = 3, z(5, 0) = 15, z(9, 0) = 27. So the minimum is 3 at (0, 3) and the maximum is 27 at (9, 0).

mcqs.q: In linear programming, the maximum or minimum of the objective function over a feasible region always occurs:
options: at the centre of the feasible region
at a corner point (vertex) of the feasible region
at every point of the region
mcqs.why: Procedure: a linear objective function takes its extreme values at the corner points of the feasible region. That is why we evaluate the function at every corner point and pick the largest (or smallest) value.

mcqs.q: The corner points of the feasible region are found by:
options: testing the point (0, 0) in each inequality
dividing the plane into half planes
taking the axes intercepts of the boundary lines and solving pairs of boundary-line equations simultaneously
mcqs.why: Corner points lie where boundary lines meet each other or meet the axes. Intercepts come from putting y = 0 and x = 0 in each associated equation, and intersection points come from solving two associated equations simultaneously.

mcqs.q: A point such as (0, 5) is a corner of the region for 5x + 4y <= 20, x >= 0, y >= 0 because:
options: it is the y-intercept of the boundary line 5x + 4y = 20, i.e. 4y = 20 gives y = 5
it lies outside the feasible region
it is the intersection of the two axes
mcqs.why: On the y-axis x = 0. Putting x = 0 in the associated equation 5x + 4y = 20 gives 4y = 20, so y = 5. The point (0, 5) is where the boundary line meets the y-axis — a corner of the feasible region.

mcqs.q: Before evaluating the objective function, the feasible region in these problems is restricted by the conditions:
options: x >= 0 and y >= 0 (the first quadrant), together with the given constraints
mcqs.why: Every problem in this exercise includes the non-negativity constraints x >= 0 and y >= 0, so the feasible region is the part of the solution region lying in the first quadrant.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 5
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 (i)

In the following, linear equation is:
(a) 5x > 7   (b) 4x - 2 < 1   (c) 2x + 1 = 1   (d) 4 = 1 + 3
Correct answer: 2x + 1 = 1

Q1 (ii)

Solution of 5x - 10 = 10 is:
(a) 0   (b) 50   (c) 4   (d) -4
Correct answer: 4

Q1 (iii)

If 7x + 4 < 6x + 6, then x belongs to the interval:
(a) (2, infinity)   (b) [2, infinity)   (c) (-infinity, 2)   (d) (-infinity, 2]
Correct answer: (-infinity, 2)

Q1 (iv)

A vertical line divides the plane into:
(a) left half plane   (b) right half plane   (c) full plane   (d) two half planes
Correct answer: two half planes

Q1 (v)

The equation formed from the linear inequality is called:
(a) cubic equation   (b) associated equation   (c) quadratic equation   (d) feasible region
Correct answer: associated equation

Q1 (vi)

3x + 4 < 0 is:
(a) equation   (b) inequality   (c) not inequality   (d) identity
Correct answer: inequality

Q1 (vii)

Corner point is also called:
(a) code   (b) vertex   (c) curve   (d) region
Correct answer: vertex

Q1 (viii)

(0, 0) is solution of inequality: [see Note in the answer of the last question of this review set — as printed, this item is defective]
(a) 4x + 5y > 8   (b) 3x + y > 6   (c) -2x + 3y < 0   (d) x + y > 4
Correct answer: -2x + 3y < 0

Q1 (ix)

The solution region restricted to the first quadrant is called:
(a) objective region   (b) feasible region   (c) solution region   (d) constraints region
Correct answer: feasible region

Q1 (x)

A function that is to be maximized or minimized is called:
(a) solution function   (b) objective function   (c) feasible function   (d) none of these
Correct answer: objective function

Q2: Solve and represent their solutions on real line

(i) (x + 5)/3 = 1 - x (ii) (2x + 1)/3 + 1/2 = 1 - (x - 1)/3 (iii) 3x + 7 < 16 (iv) 5(x - 3) >= 26x - (10x + 4)

(i) (x + 5)/3 = 1 - x: Step 1: Multiply both sides by 3: x + 5 = 3 - 3x. Step 2: Add 3x to both sides: 4x + 5 = 3. Step 3: 4x = -2. Step 4: x = -1/2. Real line: a filled dot at -1/2.

(ii) (2x + 1)/3 + 1/2 = 1 - (x - 1)/3: Step 1: Multiply every term by LCM 6: 2(2x + 1) + 3 = 6 - 2(x - 1). Step 2: 4x + 2 + 3 = 6 - 2x + 2, so 4x + 5 = 8 - 2x. Step 3: Add 2x: 6x + 5 = 8. Step 4: 6x = 3, so x = 1/2. Real line: a filled dot at 1/2.

(iii) 3x + 7 < 16: Step 1: Subtract 7: 3x < 9. Step 2: Divide by 3: x < 3. Solution: (-infinity, 3). Real line: open circle at 3, arrow to the left.

(iv) 5(x - 3) >= 26x - (10x + 4): Step 1: Expand both sides: 5x - 15 >= 26x - 10x - 4 = 16x - 4. Step 2: Subtract 16x: -11x - 15 >= -4. Step 3: Add 15: -11x >= 11. Step 4: Divide by -11 (negative, reverse the sign): x <= -1. Solution: (-infinity, -1]. Real line: filled circle at -1, arrow to the left.

Note on Review Q.1 (viii): Substituting (0, 0) in the four printed options gives 0 > 8 (false), 0 > 6 (false), 0 < 0 (false) and 0 > 4 (false) — as printed, NO option is satisfied by (0, 0), so the item is defective in the book. Option (c) is marked only because it is the one that becomes true with the slightest correction (if it were -2x + 3y <= 0). Flagged in the manifest.

Q3: Find the solution region of the following linear equalities (inequalities)

(i) 3x - 4y <= 12 ; 3x + 2y >= 3 (ii) 2x + y <= 4 ; x + 2y <= 6

Procedure as in Exercise 5.1 Q.4. [Graphs described in words — see manifest flag.]

(i) 3x - 4y <= 12 and 3x + 2y >= 3: Line 1 (3x - 4y = 12) through (4, 0), (0, -3); test (0, 0): 0 <= 12 true, take the origin side. Line 2 (3x + 2y = 3) through (1, 0), (0, 3/2); test (0, 0): 0 >= 3 false, take the side away from the origin. Corner: subtract line 2 from line 1 equations: (3x - 4y) - (3x + 2y) = 12 - 3, so -6y = 9, y = -3/2; then 3x + 2(-3/2) = 3 gives 3x = 6, x = 2. Corner point: (2, -3/2). Region: unbounded wedge.

(ii) 2x + y <= 4 and x + 2y <= 6: Line 1 (2x + y = 4) through (2, 0), (0, 4); origin side. Line 2 (x + 2y = 6) through (6, 0), (0, 3); origin side. The common region is the bounded quadrilateral with corner points (0, 0), (2, 0), (0, 3) and the intersection of the lines: from line 1, y = 4 - 2x; substitute in line 2: x + 2(4 - 2x) = 6, so -3x = -2, x = 2/3, y = 8/3: corner point (2/3, 8/3).

Q4: Find the maximum value of g(x, y) = x + 4y subject to constraints x + y <= 4, x >= 0 and y >= 0

Find the maximum value of g.

Step 1: Feasible region: below the line x + y = 4 in the first quadrant (x >= 0, y >= 0).

Step 2: Corner points: (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 4).

Step 3: Evaluate g(x, y) = x + 4y: g(0, 0) = 0; g(4, 0) = 4; g(0, 4) = 16.

Hence the maximum value of g is 16 at the corner point (0, 4).

Q5: Find the minimum value of f(x, y) = 3x + 5y subject to constraints x + 3y >= 3, x + y >= 2, x >= 0, y >= 0

Find the minimum value of f.

Step 1: Feasible region: above both lines x + 3y = 3 (intercepts (3, 0), (0, 1)) and x + y = 2 (intercepts (2, 0), (0, 2)), in the first quadrant; the region is unbounded.

Step 2: Corner points: (3, 0) (on x + 3y = 3 with y = 0; check x + y = 3 >= 2 ✓); (0, 2) (on x + y = 2 with x = 0; check x + 3y = 6 >= 3 ✓); intersection of the two lines: subtract: (x + 3y) - (x + y) = 3 - 2, so 2y = 1, y = 1/2, x = 3/2: point (3/2, 1/2).

Step 3: Evaluate f(x, y) = 3x + 5y: f(3, 0) = 9; f(0, 2) = 10; f(3/2, 1/2) = 9/2 + 5/2 = 7.

Hence the minimum value of f is 7 at the corner point (3/2, 1/2).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a linear equation?
mcqs.why: A linear equation contains an unknown to the first power joined by an equality sign. 2x + 1 = 1 qualifies; 5x > 7 and 4x - 2 < 1 are inequalities, and 4 = 1 + 3 has no unknown.

mcqs.q: The solution of 5x - 10 = 10 is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Add 10 to both sides: 5x = 20. Step 2: Divide by 5: x = 4.

mcqs.q: If 7x + 4 < 6x + 6, then x belongs to the interval:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Subtract 6x from both sides: x + 4 < 6. Step 2: Subtract 4: x < 2. So x lies in (-infinity, 2), with 2 excluded (open interval).

mcqs.q: A vertical line divides the plane into:
mcqs.why: Any straight line divides the plane into two half planes. A vertical line gives a left half plane and a right half plane.

mcqs.q: The equation formed from a linear inequality (by replacing the inequality sign with =) is called the:
mcqs.why: For example, the associated equation of 2x + y <= 6 is 2x + y = 6. Its graph is the boundary line of the solution region.

mcqs.q: 3x + 4 < 0 is an example of:
mcqs.why: It contains the sign < between two expressions and no equality, so it is an inequality in one variable x.

mcqs.q: A corner point of a feasible region is also called a:
mcqs.why: The corner points where boundary lines meet are the vertices of the feasible region, and the objective function is evaluated at these vertices.

mcqs.q: (0, 0) is a solution of the inequality:
mcqs.why: Substitute (0, 0): 4(0) + 5(0) = 0 > 8 is false; 0 > 6 is false; 0 > 4 is false; but -2(0) + 3(0) = 0 < 5 is true. Note: the printed book gives this option as -2x + 3y < 0, which yields 0 < 0 — false — so as printed no option works; that is a misprint in the book, corrected here to < 5.

mcqs.q: The solution region restricted to the first quadrant is called the:
mcqs.why: In linear programming the set of points satisfying all constraints (including x >= 0, y >= 0) is the feasible region, and the optimum is searched inside it.

mcqs.q: A function that is to be maximized or minimized is called the:
mcqs.why: Functions such as f(x, y) = 2x + 5y, whose largest or smallest value is required, are called objective functions.

mcqs.q: The solution of (x + 5)/3 = 1 - x is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Multiply both sides by 3: x + 5 = 3 - 3x. Step 2: Add 3x: 4x + 5 = 3. Step 3: 4x = -2. Step 4: x = -1/2.

mcqs.q: The solution of the inequality 3x + 7 < 16 is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Subtract 7: 3x < 9. Step 2: Divide by 3 (positive, sign unchanged): x < 3. On the real line: open circle at 3, arrow to the left.

mcqs.q: The maximum value of g(x, y) = x + 4y subject to x + y <= 4, x >= 0, y >= 0 is:
The minimum value of f(x, y) = 3x + 5y subject to x + 3y >= 3, x + y >= 2, x >= 0, y >= 0 is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Corner points: (3, 0), (0, 2) and the intersection (3/2, 1/2) of the two lines. Step 2: f(3, 0) = 9, f(0, 2) = 10, f(3/2, 1/2) = 9/2 + 5/2 = 7. The minimum is 7 at (3/2, 1/2).

mcqs.q: The solution of 5(x - 3) >= 26x - (10x + 4) is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Expand: 5x - 15 >= 16x - 4. Step 2: Subtract 16x: -11x - 15 >= -4. Step 3: Add 15: -11x >= 11. Step 4: Divide by -11 and REVERSE the sign: x <= -1.

lessons.title: Exercise 6.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: Find in which quadrant the following angles lie. Write a co-terminal angle for each

(i) 65 degrees (ii) 135 degrees (iii) -40 degrees (iv) 210 degrees (v) -150 degrees

Rule: Quadrants — 0 to 90 degrees: 1st; 90 to 180: 2nd; 180 to 270: 3rd; 270 to 360: 4th. For a negative angle, add 360 degrees to get the equivalent positive angle. Co-terminal angles differ by a multiple of 360 degrees; one co-terminal angle is found by adding 360 degrees.

(i) 65 degrees: between 0 and 90, so 1st quadrant. Co-terminal angle: 65 + 360 = 425 degrees.

(ii) 135 degrees: between 90 and 180, so 2nd quadrant. Co-terminal: 135 + 360 = 495 degrees.

(iii) -40 degrees: -40 + 360 = 320 degrees, between 270 and 360, so 4th quadrant. Co-terminal angle: 320 degrees.

(iv) 210 degrees: between 180 and 270, so 3rd quadrant. Co-terminal: 210 + 360 = 570 degrees.

(v) -150 degrees: -150 + 360 = 210 degrees, between 180 and 270, so 3rd quadrant. Co-terminal angle: 210 degrees.

Q2: Convert the following into degrees, minutes, and seconds

(i) 123.456 degrees (ii) 58.7891 degrees (iii) 90.5678 degrees

Steps: Keep the whole number part as degrees. Multiply the decimal part by 60 — the whole number part of the result is the minutes. Multiply the remaining decimal part by 60 to get the seconds.

(i) 123.456 degrees: Degrees = 123. Decimal part 0.456 x 60 = 27.36, so minutes = 27. Decimal part 0.36 x 60 = 21.6, so seconds = 21.6. Result: 123 degrees 27 minutes 21.6 seconds.

(ii) 58.7891 degrees: Degrees = 58. 0.7891 x 60 = 47.346, so minutes = 47. 0.346 x 60 = 20.76, so seconds = 20.76. Result: 58 degrees 47 minutes 20.76 seconds.

(iii) 90.5678 degrees: Degrees = 90. 0.5678 x 60 = 34.068, so minutes = 34. 0.068 x 60 = 4.08, so seconds = 4.08. Result: 90 degrees 34 minutes 4.08 seconds.

Q3: Convert the following into decimal degrees

(i) 65 deg 32 min 15 sec (ii) 42 deg 18 min 45 sec (iii) 78 deg 45 min 36 sec

Formula: Decimal degrees = degrees + (minutes / 60) + (seconds / 3600).

(i) 65 deg 32 min 15 sec: = 65 + 32/60 + 15/3600 = 65 + 0.53333 + 0.00417 = 65.5375 degrees.

(ii) 42 deg 18 min 45 sec: = 42 + 18/60 + 45/3600 = 42 + 0.3 + 0.0125 = 42.3125 degrees.

(iii) 78 deg 45 min 36 sec: = 78 + 45/60 + 36/3600 = 78 + 0.75 + 0.01 = 78.76 degrees.

Q4: Convert the following into radians

(i) 36 degrees (ii) 22.5 degrees (iii) 67.5 degrees

Formula: Radians = degrees x (pi / 180).

(i) 36 degrees = 36 x pi/180 = pi/5 rad = 0.628 rad (approx).

(ii) 22.5 degrees = 22.5 x pi/180 = pi/8 rad = 0.393 rad (approx).

(iii) 67.5 degrees = 67.5 x pi/180 = 3pi/8 rad = 1.178 rad (approx).

Q5: Convert the following into degrees

(i) pi/16 rad (ii) 11pi/5 rad (iii) 7pi/6 rad

Formula: Degrees = radians x (180 / pi).

(i) pi/16 rad = (pi/16) x (180/pi) = 180/16 = 11.25 degrees.

(ii) 11pi/5 rad = (11pi/5) x (180/pi) = 11 x 36 = 396 degrees.

(iii) 7pi/6 rad = (7pi/6) x (180/pi) = 7 x 30 = 210 degrees.

Q6: Find the arc length and area of a sector if

(i) r = 6 cm and central angle theta = pi/3 radians (ii) r = 4.8/pi cm and central angle theta = 5pi/6 radians

Formulas: Arc length l = r x theta; Area of sector A = (1/2) r^2 theta, where theta is in radians.

(i) r = 6 cm, theta = pi/3: Step 1: l = 6 x (pi/3) = 2pi = 6.28 cm (approx). Step 2: A = (1/2)(6)^2 (pi/3) = (1/2)(36)(pi/3) = 6pi = 18.85 cm^2 (approx).

(ii) r = 4.8/pi cm, theta = 5pi/6: Step 1: l = (4.8/pi) x (5pi/6) = 4.8 x 5 / 6 = 4 cm. Step 2: A = (1/2)(4.8/pi)^2 (5pi/6) = 9.6/pi = 3.06 cm^2 (approx).

Q7: If the central angle of a sector is 60 degrees and the radius of the circle is 12 cm, find the area of the sector and the percentage of the total area of the circle it represents

Find the area and the percentage.

Step 1: Convert the angle to radians: theta = 60 degrees = 60 x pi/180 = pi/3 rad.

Step 2: Formula: A = (1/2) r^2 theta = (1/2)(12)^2 (pi/3) = (1/2)(144)(pi/3) = 24pi = 75.40 cm^2 (approx).

Step 3: Percentage of the whole circle: the sector angle 60 degrees is 60/360 = 1/6 of the full turn, so the percentage = (1/6) x 100 = 16.67% (approx).

Hence the area of the sector is about 75.40 cm^2, which is about 16.67% of the total area of the circle.

Q8: Find the percentage of the area of sector subtending an angle pi/8 radians

Find the percentage.

Step 1: A full circle subtends 2pi radians at the centre, so the fraction of the circle is theta / (2pi) = (pi/8) / (2pi) = 1/16.

Step 2: Percentage = (1/16) x 100 = 6.25%.

Hence the sector is 6.25% of the area of the circle.

Q9: A circular sector of radius r = 12 cm has an angle of 150 degrees. This sector is cut out and then bent to form a cone. What is the slant height and the radius of the base of this cone?

Find the slant height and the base radius. (Hint: Arc length of sector = circumference of cone.)

Step 1: Convert the angle: 150 degrees = 150 x pi/180 = 5pi/6 rad.

Step 2: Formula: arc length l = r theta = 12 x (5pi/6) = 10pi cm.

Step 3: When the sector is bent into a cone, the radius of the sector becomes the slant height of the cone: slant height = 12 cm.

Step 4: The arc becomes the circumference of the base of the cone. If R is the base radius: 2pi R = 10pi, so R = 5 cm.

Hence the slant height is 12 cm and the radius of the base of the cone is 5 cm. [The sector figure is described in words: a sector of radius 12 cm with central angle 150 degrees at centre O.]

mcqs.q: The angle 210 degrees lies in the:
mcqs.why: Quadrants: 0-90 degrees is the 1st, 90-180 the 2nd, 180-270 the 3rd and 270-360 the 4th. Since 210 lies between 180 and 270, it is in the 3rd quadrant.

mcqs.q: The angle -150 degrees lies in the:
mcqs.why: Step 1: For a negative angle add 360 degrees: -150 + 360 = 210 degrees. Step 2: 210 degrees lies between 180 and 270, so -150 degrees is in the 3rd quadrant.

mcqs.q: A co-terminal angle of 65 degrees is:
mcqs.why: Co-terminal angles differ by a multiple of 360 degrees. Adding one full turn: 65 + 360 = 425 degrees, which is co-terminal with 65 degrees.

mcqs.q: 123.456 degrees in degrees, minutes and seconds is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Whole part = 123 degrees. Step 2: 0.456 x 60 = 27.36, so minutes = 27. Step 3: 0.36 x 60 = 21.6 seconds. Result: 123 degrees 27 minutes 21.6 seconds.

mcqs.q: 65 degrees 32 minutes 15 seconds in decimal degrees is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Decimal degrees = degrees + minutes/60 + seconds/3600. Step: = 65 + 32/60 + 15/3600 = 65 + 0.53333 + 0.00417 = 65.5375 degrees.

mcqs.q: 36 degrees in radians is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Radians = degrees x (pi/180). Step: 36 x pi/180 = pi/5 rad = 0.628 rad approximately.

mcqs.q: 7pi/6 radians in degrees is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Degrees = radians x (180/pi). Step: (7pi/6) x (180/pi) = 7 x 30 = 210 degrees.

mcqs.q: For r = 6 cm and central angle theta = pi/3 rad, the arc length is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Arc length l = r x theta (theta in radians). Step: l = 6 x (pi/3) = 2pi = 6.28 cm approximately. (18.85 cm^2 is the sector AREA, not the arc length.)

mcqs.q: A sector with central angle 60 degrees and radius 12 cm is what percentage of the whole circle?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The sector is the fraction 60/360 = 1/6 of the full turn. Step 2: Percentage = (1/6) x 100 = 16.67% approximately. Its area is (1/2)(12)^2(pi/3) = 24pi = 75.40 cm^2.

mcqs.q: A sector of radius 12 cm with angle 150 degrees is bent into a cone. The base radius of the cone is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Arc length = r theta = 12 x (5pi/6) = 10pi cm. Step 2: This arc becomes the circumference of the cone's base: 2pi R = 10pi, so R = 5 cm. The slant height of the cone is the sector radius, 12 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 6.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: For each of the following right-angled triangles, find the trigonometric ratios: (i) sin theta (ii) cos theta (iii) tan theta (iv) sec theta (v) cosec theta (vi) cot phi (vii) tan phi (viii) cosec phi (ix) sec phi (x) cos phi

Triangles: (a) sides 4, 3, hypotenuse 5; (b) sides 8, 15, hypotenuse 17; (c) sides 5, 12, hypotenuse 13 (right angle at B in each; theta at A, phi at C).

Formulas (angle theta at A, right angle at B, hypotenuse AC): sin = Perpendicular/Hypotenuse, cos = Base/Hypotenuse, tan = Perpendicular/Base, and cosec, sec, cot are their reciprocals. Triangle (a): CB = 4, BA = 3, AC = 5. Triangle (b): CB = 8, BA = 15, AC = 17. Triangle (c): CB = 5, BA = 12, AC = 13. For angle phi at C, the perpendicular is BA and the base is CB.

(a) (i) sin theta = 4/5. (ii) cos theta = 3/5. (iii) tan theta = 4/3. (iv) sec theta = 5/3. (v) cosec theta = 5/4. (vi) cot phi = 4/3. (vii) tan phi = 3/4. (viii) cosec phi = 5/3. (ix) sec phi = 5/4. (x) cos phi = 4/5.

(b) (i) sin theta = 8/17. (ii) cos theta = 15/17. (iii) tan theta = 8/15. (iv) sec theta = 17/15. (v) cosec theta = 17/8. (vi) cot phi = 8/15. (vii) tan phi = 15/8. (viii) cosec phi = 17/15. (ix) sec phi = 17/8. (x) cos phi = 8/17.

(c) (i) sin theta = 5/13. (ii) cos theta = 12/13. (iii) tan theta = 5/12. (iv) sec theta = 13/12. (v) cosec theta = 13/5. (vi) cot phi = 5/12. (vii) tan phi = 12/5. (viii) cosec phi = 13/12. (ix) sec phi = 13/5. (x) cos phi = 5/13.

[The three triangles are described in words: each is right-angled at B with A at the lower right, C at the top, theta at A and phi at C.]

Q2: For the following right-angled triangle ABC find the trigonometric ratios for which angle at A = phi and angle at C = theta: (i) sin theta (ii) cos theta (iii) tan theta (iv) sin phi (v) cos phi (vi) tan phi

Triangle ABC is right-angled at B, with BC = a, AB = c and hypotenuse AC = b.

In the figure, triangle ABC is right-angled at B; side BC = a (top side), side AB = c (left side), hypotenuse AC = b. Angle at A is phi and angle at C is theta.

For theta (at C): perpendicular = AB = c, base = BC = a, hypotenuse = b.
(i) sin theta = c/b. (ii) cos theta = a/b. (iii) tan theta = c/a.

For phi (at A): perpendicular = BC = a, base = AB = c, hypotenuse = b.
(iv) sin phi = a/b. (v) cos phi = c/b. (vi) tan phi = a/c.

Q3: Considering the adjoining triangle ABC, verify that: (i) sin theta cosec theta = 1 (ii) cos theta sec theta = 1 (iii) tan theta cot theta = 1

The triangle is right-angled at C with sides 3, 4 and hypotenuse 5, theta at A.

From the figure, triangle ABC is right-angled at C, with BC = 3, AC = 4, hypotenuse AB = 5, and theta at A. For theta: perpendicular = BC = 3, base = AC = 4, hypotenuse = 5. So sin theta = 3/5, cosec theta = 5/3; cos theta = 4/5, sec theta = 5/4; tan theta = 3/4, cot theta = 4/3.

(i) sin theta x cosec theta = (3/5)(5/3) = 1 ✓.

(ii) cos theta x sec theta = (4/5)(5/4) = 1 ✓.

(iii) tan theta x cot theta = (3/4)(4/3) = 1 ✓.

Hence all three are verified (each ratio multiplied by its reciprocal gives 1).

Q4: Fill in the blanks

(i) sin 30 = sin(90 - 60) = ___ (ii) cos 30 = cos(90 - 60) = ___ (iii) tan 30 = tan(90 - 60) = ___ (iv) tan 60 = tan(90 - 30) = ___ (v) sin 60 = sin(90 - 30) = ___ (vi) cos 60 = cos(90 - 30) = ___ (vii) sin 45 = sin(90 - 45) = ___ (viii) tan 45 = tan(90 - 45) = ___ (ix) cos 45 = cos(90 - 45) = ___

Formulas (complementary angles): sin(90 - theta) = cos theta; cos(90 - theta) = sin theta; tan(90 - theta) = cot theta. Standard values: sin 30 = cos 60 = 1/2; cos 30 = sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2; tan 30 = cot 60 = 1/sqrt(3); tan 60 = cot 30 = sqrt(3); sin 45 = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2); tan 45 = cot 45 = 1.

(i) sin 30 = sin(90 - 60) = cos 60 = 1/2.

(ii) cos 30 = cos(90 - 60) = sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2.

(iii) tan 30 = tan(90 - 60) = cot 60 = 1/sqrt(3).

(iv) tan 60 = tan(90 - 30) = cot 30 = sqrt(3).

(v) sin 60 = sin(90 - 30) = cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2.

(vi) cos 60 = cos(90 - 30) = sin 30 = 1/2.

(vii) sin 45 = sin(90 - 45) = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2).

(viii) tan 45 = tan(90 - 45) = cot 45 = 1.

(ix) cos 45 = cos(90 - 45) = sin 45 = 1/sqrt(2).

Q5: In a right angled triangle ABC, angle at B = 90 degrees and C is an acute angle of 60 degrees. Also sin(angle A) = a/b, then find: (i) mBC/mAB (ii) cos 60 (iii) tan 60 (iv) cosec pi/3 (v) cot 60 (vi) sin 30 (vii) cos 30 (viii) tan pi/6 (ix) sec 30 (x) cot 30

Sides: AB = b (hypotenuse), BC = a, AC = c.

In the figure, triangle ABC is right-angled at B, angle at C is 60 degrees, so angle at A is 30 degrees. Sides: hypotenuse AB = b, base BC = a, perpendicular AC = c. It is given that sin(angle A) = a/b; but sin 30 = 1/2, so a/b = 1/2, i.e. b = 2a. By Pythagoras: c^2 = b^2 - a^2 = 4a^2 - a^2 = 3a^2, so c = a sqrt(3).

(i) mBC / mAB = a/b = 1/2.

(ii) cos 60 = base/hypotenuse for angle C = a/b = 1/2.

(iii) tan 60 = perpendicular/base for angle C = c/a = sqrt(3).

(iv) cosec(pi/3) = cosec 60 = 1/sin 60 = 2/sqrt(3).

(v) cot 60 = base/perpendicular = a/c = 1/sqrt(3).

(vi) sin 30 = a/b = 1/2.

(vii) cos 30 = c/b = sqrt(3)/2.

(viii) tan(pi/6) = tan 30 = a/c = 1/sqrt(3).

(ix) sec 30 = b/c = 2/sqrt(3).

(x) cot 30 = c/a = sqrt(3).

mcqs.q: In a right-angled triangle with sides 3, 4 and hypotenuse 5, for the angle theta opposite the side 4, sin theta is:
mcqs.why: Formula: sin = Perpendicular/Hypotenuse. For theta the perpendicular (opposite side) is 4 and the hypotenuse is 5, so sin theta = 4/5.

mcqs.q: For the same 3-4-5 triangle, tan theta (theta opposite the side 4) is:
mcqs.why: Formula: tan = Perpendicular/Base. The perpendicular is 4 and the base (adjacent side) is 3, so tan theta = 4/3.

mcqs.q: In a right-angled triangle with sides 8, 15 and hypotenuse 17, cos theta for the angle opposite the side 8 is:
mcqs.why: Formula: cos = Base/Hypotenuse. For the angle opposite the side 8, the base is 15 and the hypotenuse is 17, so cos theta = 15/17.

mcqs.q: sec theta is the reciprocal of:
mcqs.why: The reciprocal pairs are: cosec = 1/sin, sec = 1/cos and cot = 1/tan. So sec theta = 1/cos theta; for the 3-4-5 triangle with cos theta = 3/5, sec theta = 5/3.

mcqs.q: sin(90 degrees - theta) is equal to:
mcqs.why: Complementary-angle formula: sin(90 - theta) = cos theta. Similarly cos(90 - theta) = sin theta and tan(90 - theta) = cot theta.

mcqs.q: tan 60 degrees is equal to:
mcqs.why: From the 30-60-90 triangle: tan 60 = perpendicular/base = sqrt(3)/1 = sqrt(3). Also tan 60 = cot 30 by the complementary-angle formula.

mcqs.q: sin 45 degrees is equal to:
mcqs.why: From the 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1, 1 and hypotenuse sqrt(2): sin 45 = 1/sqrt(2). Note cos 45 has the same value, 1/sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: cosec 60 degrees is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2. Step 2: cosec is the reciprocal of sin: cosec 60 = 1/(sqrt(3)/2) = 2/sqrt(3). In radians this is cosec(pi/3).

mcqs.q: cot 30 degrees is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3). Step 2: cot is the reciprocal of tan: cot 30 = sqrt(3). This also equals tan 60 by the complementary-angle formula.

mcqs.q: For any acute angle theta, sin theta x cosec theta equals:
mcqs.why: cosec theta = 1/sin theta, so sin theta x cosec theta = sin theta x (1/sin theta) = 1. The same holds for cos theta x sec theta and tan theta x cot theta.

lessons.title: Exercise 6.3
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: If theta lies in first quadrant, find the remaining trigonometric ratios of theta

(i) sin theta = 2/3 (ii) cos theta = 3/4 (iii) tan theta = 1/2 (iv) sec theta = 3 (v) cot theta = sqrt(3/2)

Method: Use Formula: sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1 to find the sine/cosine, then tan theta = sin theta / cos theta, and take reciprocals for cosec, sec, cot. Theta is in the first quadrant, so all ratios are positive.

(i) sin theta = 2/3: Step 1: cos^2 theta = 1 - (2/3)^2 = 1 - 4/9 = 5/9, so cos theta = sqrt(5)/3. Step 2: tan theta = (2/3)/(sqrt(5)/3) = 2/sqrt(5). Step 3: cot theta = sqrt(5)/2; sec theta = 3/sqrt(5); cosec theta = 3/2.

(ii) cos theta = 3/4: Step 1: sin^2 theta = 1 - 9/16 = 7/16, so sin theta = sqrt(7)/4. Step 2: tan theta = sqrt(7)/3. Step 3: cot theta = 3/sqrt(7); sec theta = 4/3; cosec theta = 4/sqrt(7).

(iii) tan theta = 1/2: Step 1: Formula: sec^2 theta = 1 + tan^2 theta = 1 + 1/4 = 5/4, so sec theta = sqrt(5)/2 and cos theta = 2/sqrt(5). Step 2: sin theta = tan theta x cos theta = (1/2)(2/sqrt(5)) = 1/sqrt(5). Step 3: cot theta = 2; cosec theta = sqrt(5).

(iv) sec theta = 3: Step 1: cos theta = 1/3. Step 2: sin^2 theta = 1 - 1/9 = 8/9, so sin theta = 2 sqrt(2)/3. Step 3: tan theta = sin/cos = 2 sqrt(2); cot theta = 1/(2 sqrt(2)); cosec theta = 3/(2 sqrt(2)).

(v) cot theta = sqrt(3/2): Step 1: tan theta = 1/cot theta = sqrt(2/3). Step 2: Formula: cosec^2 theta = 1 + cot^2 theta = 1 + 3/2 = 5/2, so cosec theta = sqrt(5/2) and sin theta = sqrt(2/5). Step 3: Formula: sec^2 theta = 1 + tan^2 theta = 1 + 2/3 = 5/3, so sec theta = sqrt(5/3) and cos theta = sqrt(3/5).

Q2 to Q.12: Prove the following trigonometric identities

2. (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta 3. cos theta / sin theta = 1/tan theta 4. sin theta/cosec theta + cos theta/sec theta = 1 5. cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta = 2 cos^2 theta - 1 6. cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta = 1 - 2 sin^2 theta 7. (1 - sin theta)/cos theta = cos theta/(1 + sin theta) 8. (sec theta - tan theta)^2 = (1 - sin theta)/(1 + sin theta) 9. (tan theta + cot theta)^2 = sec^2 theta cosec^2 theta 10. (tan theta + sec theta - 1)/(tan theta - sec theta + 1) = tan theta + sec theta 11. sin^3 theta - cos^3 theta = (sin theta - cos theta)(1 + sin theta cos theta) 12. sin^6 theta - cos^6 theta = (sin^2 theta - cos^2 theta)(1 - sin^2 theta cos^2 theta)

2. L.H.S = (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = sin^2 theta + 2 sin theta cos theta + cos^2 theta [Formula: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2] = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta [Formula: sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1] = R.H.S. Hence proved.

3. R.H.S = 1/tan theta = 1 / (sin theta / cos theta) = cos theta / sin theta = L.H.S. Hence proved.

4. L.H.S = sin theta/cosec theta + cos theta/sec theta = sin theta x sin theta + cos theta x cos theta [since 1/cosec theta = sin theta and 1/sec theta = cos theta] = sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1 = R.H.S. Hence proved.

5. L.H.S = cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta = cos^2 theta - (1 - cos^2 theta) [Formula: sin^2 theta = 1 - cos^2 theta] = 2 cos^2 theta - 1 = R.H.S. Hence proved.

6. L.H.S = cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta = (1 - sin^2 theta) - sin^2 theta [Formula: cos^2 theta = 1 - sin^2 theta] = 1 - 2 sin^2 theta = R.H.S. Hence proved.

7. R.H.S = cos theta / (1 + sin theta). Multiply numerator and denominator by (1 - sin theta): = cos theta (1 - sin theta) / [(1 + sin theta)(1 - sin theta)] = cos theta (1 - sin theta) / (1 - sin^2 theta) = cos theta (1 - sin theta) / cos^2 theta = (1 - sin theta)/cos theta = L.H.S. Hence proved.

8. R.H.S = (1 - sin theta)/(1 + sin theta). L.H.S = (sec theta - tan theta)^2 = (1/cos theta - sin theta/cos theta)^2 = [(1 - sin theta)/cos theta]^2 = (1 - sin theta)^2 / cos^2 theta = (1 - sin theta)^2 / (1 - sin^2 theta) = (1 - sin theta)^2 / [(1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta)] = (1 - sin theta)/(1 + sin theta) = R.H.S. Hence proved.

9. L.H.S = (tan theta + cot theta)^2 = (sin theta/cos theta + cos theta/sin theta)^2 = [(sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta)/(sin theta cos theta)]^2 = [1/(sin theta cos theta)]^2 = 1/(sin^2 theta cos^2 theta) = (1/sin^2 theta)(1/cos^2 theta) = cosec^2 theta sec^2 theta = R.H.S. Hence proved.

10. L.H.S = (tan theta + sec theta - 1)/(tan theta - sec theta + 1). Write 1 = sec^2 theta - tan^2 theta in the numerator: numerator = (tan theta + sec theta) - (sec^2 theta - tan^2 theta) = (tan theta + sec theta) - (sec theta - tan theta)(sec theta + tan theta) = (sec theta + tan theta)[1 - (sec theta - tan theta)] = (sec theta + tan theta)(1 - sec theta + tan theta). Denominator = tan theta - sec theta + 1 = (1 - sec theta + tan theta). Cancelling the common factor: L.H.S = sec theta + tan theta = tan theta + sec theta = R.H.S. Hence proved.

11. R.H.S = (sin theta - cos theta)(1 + sin theta cos theta). L.H.S = sin^3 theta - cos^3 theta = (sin theta - cos theta)(sin^2 theta + sin theta cos theta + cos^2 theta) [Formula: a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)] = (sin theta - cos theta)(1 + sin theta cos theta) = R.H.S. Hence proved.

12. L.H.S = sin^6 theta - cos^6 theta = (sin^2 theta)^3 - (cos^2 theta)^3 = (sin^2 theta - cos^2 theta)(sin^4 theta + sin^2 theta cos^2 theta + cos^4 theta) [Formula: a^3 - b^3]. Now sin^4 theta + cos^4 theta = (sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta)^2 - 2 sin^2 theta cos^2 theta = 1 - 2 sin^2 theta cos^2 theta, so the second factor = 1 - 2 sin^2 theta cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta cos^2 theta = 1 - sin^2 theta cos^2 theta. Hence L.H.S = (sin^2 theta - cos^2 theta)(1 - sin^2 theta cos^2 theta) = R.H.S. Hence proved.

mcqs.q: If sin theta = 2/3 and theta is in the first quadrant, then cos theta is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula: sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1, so cos^2 theta = 1 - (2/3)^2 = 1 - 4/9 = 5/9. Step 2: In the first quadrant cos is positive: cos theta = sqrt(5)/3.

mcqs.q: If sin theta = 2/3 (first quadrant), then tan theta is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: cos theta = sqrt(5)/3 (from sin^2 + cos^2 = 1). Step 2: Formula: tan theta = sin theta / cos theta = (2/3)/(sqrt(5)/3) = 2/sqrt(5).

mcqs.q: If cos theta = 3/4 (first quadrant), then sin theta is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula: sin^2 theta = 1 - cos^2 theta = 1 - 9/16 = 7/16. Step 2: First quadrant, so sin theta = sqrt(7)/4 (positive).

mcqs.q: If tan theta = 1/2 (first quadrant), then sec theta is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula: sec^2 theta = 1 + tan^2 theta = 1 + 1/4 = 5/4. Step 2: First quadrant: sec theta = sqrt(5)/2, and hence cos theta = 2/sqrt(5).

mcqs.q: If sec theta = 3 (first quadrant), then tan theta is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: cos theta = 1/sec theta = 1/3. Step 2: sin^2 theta = 1 - 1/9 = 8/9, so sin theta = 2 sqrt(2)/3. Step 3: tan theta = sin/cos = (2 sqrt(2)/3)/(1/3) = 2 sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: (sin theta + cos theta)^2 simplifies to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2: = sin^2 theta + 2 sin theta cos theta + cos^2 theta. Step 2: Formula sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1 gives 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta.

mcqs.q: cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Replace sin^2 theta by 1 - cos^2 theta: cos^2 theta - (1 - cos^2 theta) = 2 cos^2 theta - 1. Step 2: Replacing cos^2 theta by 1 - sin^2 theta instead gives the equal form 1 - 2 sin^2 theta.

mcqs.q: sin theta/cosec theta + cos theta/sec theta is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1/cosec theta = sin theta and 1/sec theta = cos theta, so the expression = sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta. Step 2: By the fundamental identity this equals 1.

mcqs.q: (tan theta + cot theta)^2 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: tan + cot = (sin^2 + cos^2)/(sin cos) = 1/(sin theta cos theta). Step 2: Squaring: 1/(sin^2 theta cos^2 theta) = (1/sin^2 theta)(1/cos^2 theta) = cosec^2 theta sec^2 theta.

mcqs.q: sin^3 theta - cos^3 theta factorized (as used in the identity proof) is:
options: (sin theta - cos theta)(1 - sin theta cos theta)
(sin theta - cos theta)(1 + sin theta cos theta)
(sin theta + cos theta)(1 + sin theta cos theta)
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2): = (sin theta - cos theta)(sin^2 theta + sin theta cos theta + cos^2 theta). Step 2: sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, so the second factor is (1 + sin theta cos theta).

lessons.title: Exercise 6.4
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: Find the value of the following trigonometric ratios without using the calculator

(i) sin 30 (ii) cos 30 (iii) tan pi/6 (iv) tan 60 (v) sec 60 (vi) cos pi/3 (vii) cot 60 (viii) sin 60 (ix) sec 30 (x) cosec 30 (xi) sin 45 (xii) cos pi/4

Standard values (from the 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles): sin 30 = 1/2, cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2, tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3); sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2, cos 60 = 1/2, tan 60 = sqrt(3); sin 45 = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2); and the reciprocals for sec, cosec, cot. Also pi/6 rad = 30 degrees, pi/3 rad = 60 degrees, pi/4 rad = 45 degrees.

(i) sin 30 = 1/2. (ii) cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2. (iii) tan(pi/6) = tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3). (iv) tan 60 = sqrt(3). (v) sec 60 = 1/cos 60 = 2. (vi) cos(pi/3) = cos 60 = 1/2. (vii) cot 60 = 1/tan 60 = 1/sqrt(3). (viii) sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2. (ix) sec 30 = 1/cos 30 = 2/sqrt(3). (x) cosec 30 = 1/sin 30 = 2. (xi) sin 45 = 1/sqrt(2). (xii) cos(pi/4) = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2).

Q2: Evaluate

(i) 2 sin 60 cos 60 (ii) 2 cos(pi/6) sin(pi/6) (iii) 2 sin 45 + 2 cos 45 (iv) sin 60 cos 30 + cos 60 sin 30 (v) cos 60 cos 30 - sin 60 sin 30 (vi) sin 60 cos 30 - cos 60 sin 30 (vii) cos 60 cos 30 + sin 60 sin 30 (viii) tan(pi/6) cot(pi/6) + 1

Substitute the standard values and simplify.

(i) 2 sin 60 cos 60 = 2 x (sqrt(3)/2) x (1/2) = sqrt(3)/2.

(ii) 2 cos(pi/6) sin(pi/6) = 2 cos 30 sin 30 = 2 x (sqrt(3)/2) x (1/2) = sqrt(3)/2.

(iii) 2 sin 45 + 2 cos 45 = 2(1/sqrt(2)) + 2(1/sqrt(2)) = 4/sqrt(2) = 2 sqrt(2).

(iv) sin 60 cos 30 + cos 60 sin 30 = (sqrt(3)/2)(sqrt(3)/2) + (1/2)(1/2) = 3/4 + 1/4 = 1.

(v) cos 60 cos 30 - sin 60 sin 30 = (1/2)(sqrt(3)/2) - (sqrt(3)/2)(1/2) = sqrt(3)/4 - sqrt(3)/4 = 0.

(vi) sin 60 cos 30 - cos 60 sin 30 = 3/4 - 1/4 = 1/2.

(vii) cos 60 cos 30 + sin 60 sin 30 = sqrt(3)/4 + sqrt(3)/4 = sqrt(3)/2.

(viii) tan(pi/6) cot(pi/6) + 1 = tan 30 cot 30 + 1 = (1/sqrt(3))(sqrt(3)) + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2.

Q3: If sin pi/4 and cos pi/4 equal to 1/sqrt(2) each, then find the value of the followings

(i) 2 sin 45 - 2 cos 45 (ii) 3 cos 45 + 4 sin 45 (iii) 5 cos 45 - 3 sin 45

Given sin(pi/4) = cos(pi/4) = 1/sqrt(2), i.e. sin 45 = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2).

(i) 2 sin 45 - 2 cos 45 = 2(1/sqrt(2)) - 2(1/sqrt(2)) = 0.

(ii) 3 cos 45 + 4 sin 45 = 3(1/sqrt(2)) + 4(1/sqrt(2)) = 7/sqrt(2) = 7 sqrt(2)/2.

(iii) 5 cos 45 - 3 sin 45 = 5(1/sqrt(2)) - 3(1/sqrt(2)) = 2/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: sin 30 degrees is:
mcqs.why: From the 30-60-90 triangle (sides 1, sqrt(3), 2): sin 30 = opposite/hypotenuse = 1/2.

mcqs.q: tan(pi/6) is:
mcqs.why: pi/6 rad = 30 degrees. tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3) from the standard 30-60-90 triangle values.

mcqs.q: sec 60 degrees is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: cos 60 = 1/2. Step 2: sec is the reciprocal of cos: sec 60 = 1/(1/2) = 2.

mcqs.q: cosec 30 degrees is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: sin 30 = 1/2. Step 2: cosec is the reciprocal of sin: cosec 30 = 1/(1/2) = 2.

mcqs.q: 2 sin 60 cos 60 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step: Substitute the standard values: 2 x (sqrt(3)/2) x (1/2) = sqrt(3)/2.

mcqs.q: sin 60 cos 30 + cos 60 sin 30 is equal to:
cos 60 cos 30 - sin 60 sin 30 is equal to:
2 sin 45 + 2 cos 45 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: sin 45 = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2). Step 2: 2(1/sqrt(2)) + 2(1/sqrt(2)) = 4/sqrt(2). Step 3: Rationalize: 4/sqrt(2) = 2 sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: tan(pi/6) cot(pi/6) + 1 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: tan and cot are reciprocals, so tan(pi/6) cot(pi/6) = 1. Step 2: 1 + 1 = 2.

mcqs.q: 3 cos 45 + 4 sin 45 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: cos 45 = sin 45 = 1/sqrt(2). Step 2: 3(1/sqrt(2)) + 4(1/sqrt(2)) = 7/sqrt(2) = 7 sqrt(2)/2 after rationalizing.

lessons.title: Exercise 6.5
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: Find the values of x, y and z from the following right angled triangles

(i) angle at A = 30 degrees, y = 4 cm (ii) angle at A = pi/4, one side = sqrt(3) cm (iii) angle at C = 60 degrees, z = 2 cm (iv) angle at A = 45 degrees, y = 4 cm

In each figure, triangle ABC is right-angled at B, angle at A is given, CB = x, AB = y, AC = z. Formulas: tan(angle A) = x/y, cos(angle A) = y/z, sin(angle A) = x/z.

(i) Angle A = 30 degrees, y = 4 cm: Step 1: tan 30 = x/4, so x = 4 x (1/sqrt(3)) = 4/sqrt(3) = 2.31 cm (approx). Step 2: cos 30 = 4/z, so z = 4/(sqrt(3)/2) = 8/sqrt(3) = 4.62 cm (approx).

(ii) Angle A = pi/4 = 45 degrees, perpendicular CB = sqrt(3) cm (the side labelled with value sqrt(3) cm), base AB = x, hypotenuse AC = z: Step 1: tan 45 = sqrt(3)/x, so x = sqrt(3)/1 = sqrt(3) = 1.73 cm. Step 2: sin 45 = sqrt(3)/z, so z = sqrt(3)/(1/sqrt(2)) = sqrt(6) = 2.45 cm (approx).

(iii) Triangle with right angle at B, angle at C = 60 degrees, hypotenuse AC = z = 2 cm, base CB = x, perpendicular AB = y: Step 1: cos 60 = x/2, so x = 2 x (1/2) = 1 cm. Step 2: sin 60 = y/2, so y = 2 x (sqrt(3)/2) = sqrt(3) = 1.73 cm.

(iv) Angle A = 45 degrees, y = 4 cm: Step 1: tan 45 = x/4, so x = 4 cm. Step 2: cos 45 = 4/z, so z = 4 sqrt(2) = 5.66 cm (approx).

Q2: Find the unknown side and angles of the following triangles

(i) a = sqrt(3) cm, c = sqrt(13) cm (ii) a = 4 cm, c = 4 cm (both right-angled at B)

(i) Triangle right-angled at B with a = CB = sqrt(3) cm, c = AB = sqrt(13) cm, b = AC (hypotenuse): Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): b^2 = a^2 + c^2 = 3 + 13 = 16, so b = 4 cm. Step 2: sin(angle A) = a/b = sqrt(3)/4 = 0.433, so angle A = sin^-1(0.433) = 25.66 degrees (approx). Step 3: angle C = 90 - 25.66 = 64.34 degrees (approx). Unknowns: b = 4 cm, angle A = 25.66 degrees, angle C = 64.34 degrees.

(ii) Triangle right-angled at B with a = CB = 4 cm, c = AB = 4 cm: Step 1: b^2 = 16 + 16 = 32, so b = 4 sqrt(2) = 5.66 cm (approx). Step 2: tan(angle A) = a/c = 4/4 = 1, so angle A = 45 degrees. Step 3: angle C = 90 - 45 = 45 degrees. Unknowns: b = 5.66 cm, angle A = angle C = 45 degrees.

Q3: Each side of a square field is 60 m long. Find the lengths of the diagonals of the field

Find the diagonal length.

Step 1: The diagonal of a square of side s forms a right-angled triangle with two sides, so by Pythagoras: diagonal^2 = s^2 + s^2 = 2s^2.

Step 2: diagonal = s sqrt(2) = 60 sqrt(2) = 84.85 m (approx).

Hence each diagonal of the field is 60 sqrt(2) m, about 84.85 m long.

Q4: Solve the following triangles when angle B = 90 degrees

(i) angle C = 60 degrees, c = 3 sqrt(3) cm (ii) angle C = 45 degrees, a = 8 cm (iii) a = 12 cm, c = 6 cm (iv) angle A = 60 degrees, c = 4 cm (v) angle A = 30 degrees, c = 4 cm (vi) b = 10 cm, a = 6 cm

Notation: triangle ABC with angle B = 90 degrees; a = BC (opposite A), b = AC (hypotenuse), c = AB (opposite C). Formulas: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent; Pythagoras: b^2 = a^2 + c^2.

(i) Angle C = 60 degrees, c = 3 sqrt(3) cm: Step 1: Angle A = 90 - 60 = 30 degrees. Step 2: tan 60 = c/a, so a = c/tan 60 = 3 sqrt(3)/sqrt(3) = 3 cm. Step 3: sin 60 = c/b, so b = c/sin 60 = 3 sqrt(3)/(sqrt(3)/2) = 6 cm. Solution: angle A = 30 degrees, a = 3 cm, b = 6 cm.

(ii) Angle C = 45 degrees, a = 8 cm: Step 1: Angle A = 45 degrees. Step 2: tan 45 = a/c, so c = a/tan 45 = 8 cm. Step 3: sin 45 = a/b, so b = 8/(1/sqrt(2)) = 8 sqrt(2) = 11.31 cm (approx). Solution: angle A = 45 degrees, c = 8 cm, b = 11.31 cm.

(iii) a = 12 cm, c = 6 cm: Step 1: b = sqrt(a^2 + c^2) = sqrt(144 + 36) = sqrt(180) = 6 sqrt(5) = 13.42 cm (approx). Step 2: tan(angle A) = a/c = 12/6 = 2, so angle A = tan^-1(2) = 63.43 degrees (approx). Step 3: angle C = 90 - 63.43 = 26.57 degrees (approx).

(iv) Angle A = 60 degrees, c = 4 cm: Step 1: Angle C = 30 degrees. Step 2: tan 60 = a/c, so a = 4 sqrt(3) = 6.93 cm (approx). Step 3: cos 60 = c/b, so b = 4/(1/2) = 8 cm.

(v) Angle A = 30 degrees, c = 4 cm: Step 1: Angle C = 60 degrees. Step 2: tan 30 = a/c, so a = 4/sqrt(3) = 2.31 cm (approx). Step 3: cos 30 = c/b, so b = 4/(sqrt(3)/2) = 8/sqrt(3) = 4.62 cm (approx).

(vi) b = 10 cm, a = 6 cm: Step 1: c = sqrt(b^2 - a^2) = sqrt(100 - 36) = sqrt(64) = 8 cm. Step 2: sin(angle A) = a/b = 6/10 = 0.6, so angle A = sin^-1(0.6) = 36.87 degrees (approx). Step 3: angle C = 90 - 36.87 = 53.13 degrees (approx).

Q5: Let Q and R be the two points on the same bank of a canal. The point P is placed on the other bank straight to point R. Find the width of the canal and the angle PQR in radians

From the figure: QR = 5 m, PQ = 13 m, right angle at R.

In the figure, P and R are on opposite banks, Q and R on the same bank, the angle at R is a right angle, QR = 5 m along the bank and PQ = 13 m across (hypotenuse). The width of the canal is PR.

Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): PR^2 = PQ^2 - QR^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144.

Step 2: PR = 12 m. So the width of the canal is 12 m.

Step 3: For angle PQR at Q: sin(angle PQR) = opposite/hypotenuse = PR/PQ = 12/13, so angle PQR = sin^-1(12/13) = 67.38 degrees (approx).

Step 4: Convert to radians: 67.38 x pi/180 = 1.176 rad (approx).

Hence the width of the canal is 12 m and angle PQR is about 1.176 radians.

Q6: Calculate the length x in the adjoining figure

Figure: AB = 10 cm, CD = 8 cm, AD = 17 cm, right angles at B (in triangle ABD) and at C.

In the figure, ABCD is a quadrilateral with A at the lower left, B at the upper left-middle, C at the upper right (right angle at C), D at the lower right; AB = 10 cm, CD = 8 cm, AD = 17 cm, BC = x, and the diagonal BD makes a right angle at B in triangle ABD (angle ABD = 90 degrees).

Step 1: In right-angled triangle ABD, Formula (Pythagoras): BD^2 = AD^2 - AB^2 = 17^2 - 10^2 = 289 - 100 = 189, so BD = sqrt(189) = 3 sqrt(21) = 13.75 cm (approx).

Step 2: In right-angled triangle BCD (right angle at C): BC^2 = BD^2 - CD^2 = 189 - 64 = 125.

Step 3: x = BC = sqrt(125) = 5 sqrt(5) = 11.18 cm (approx).

Q7: If the ladder is placed along the wall such that the foot of the ladder is 2 m away from the wall. If the length of the ladder is 8 m, find the height of the wall

Find the height reached.

The ladder, the wall and the ground form a right-angled triangle: ladder = hypotenuse = 8 m, distance of the foot from the wall = base = 2 m, height of the wall reached = perpendicular h.

Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): h^2 = 8^2 - 2^2 = 64 - 4 = 60.

Step 2: h = sqrt(60) = 2 sqrt(15) = 7.75 m (approx).

Hence the ladder reaches about 7.75 m up the wall.

Q8: The diagonal of a rectangular field ABCD is (x + 9) m and the sides are (x + 7) m and x m. Find the value of x

Find x.

For rectangle ABCD, the diagonal AC, length (x + 9) m, is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle with sides (x + 7) m and x m.

Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): (x + 9)^2 = (x + 7)^2 + x^2.

Step 2: Expand: x^2 + 18x + 81 = x^2 + 14x + 49 + x^2.

Step 3: Bring all terms to one side: 0 = x^2 - 4x - 32.

Step 4: Factorize: x^2 - 4x - 32 = (x - 8)(x + 4) = 0, so x = 8 or x = -4.

Step 5: Length cannot be negative, so x = 8.

Q9: Calculate the value of x in each case

(i) Right-angled triangle, legs/hypotenuse 12 cm and 20 cm, third side x (ii) Two right triangles on a common altitude DB, AB = BC = 4 cm, DC = 8 cm, AD = x

(i) Triangle ABC is right-angled at B, AB = 12 cm, hypotenuse AC = 20 cm, BC = x: Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): x^2 = AC^2 - AB^2 = 400 - 144 = 256. Step 2: x = 16 cm.

(ii) In the figure, D is the top vertex, DB is perpendicular to AC at B, AB = BC with BC = 4 cm (so AB = 4 cm), AD = x cm, DC = 8 cm: Step 1: In right-angled triangle DBC: BD^2 = DC^2 - BC^2 = 64 - 16 = 48. Step 2: In right-angled triangle ABD: BD^2 = AD^2 - AB^2 = x^2 - 16. Step 3: Equate: x^2 - 16 = 48, so x^2 = 64 and x = 8 cm.

mcqs.q: Each side of a square field is 60 m. The length of each diagonal is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 60 and 60: diagonal^2 = 60^2 + 60^2 = 2 x 60^2 (Pythagoras). Step 2: diagonal = 60 sqrt(2) = 84.85 m approximately.

mcqs.q: In a right triangle (angle B = 90 degrees) with b = 10 cm and a = 6 cm, the side c is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): c = sqrt(b^2 - a^2) since b is the hypotenuse. Step 2: = sqrt(100 - 36) = sqrt(64) = 8 cm.

mcqs.q: A ladder 8 m long has its foot 2 m from a wall. The height it reaches up the wall is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): h^2 = 8^2 - 2^2 = 64 - 4 = 60. Step 2: h = sqrt(60) = 2 sqrt(15) = 7.75 m approximately.

mcqs.q: The diagonal of a rectangular field is (x + 9) m and its sides are (x + 7) m and x m. The value of x is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Pythagoras: (x + 9)^2 = (x + 7)^2 + x^2. Step 2: Expanding and simplifying: 0 = x^2 - 4x - 32 = (x - 8)(x + 4). Step 3: x = 8 or x = -4; length cannot be negative, so x = 8.

mcqs.q: Points Q, R are on one bank of a canal and P is opposite R, with QR = 5 m, PQ = 13 m and a right angle at R. The width of the canal PR is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): PR^2 = PQ^2 - QR^2 = 169 - 25 = 144. Step 2: PR = 12 m, the width of the canal.

mcqs.q: In a right triangle with angle A = 30 degrees and base y = 4 cm, the hypotenuse z is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula: cos(angle A) = base/hypotenuse, so cos 30 = 4/z. Step 2: z = 4/cos 30 = 4/(sqrt(3)/2) = 8/sqrt(3) = 4.62 cm approximately.

mcqs.q: Solve the triangle with angle B = 90 degrees, angle C = 60 degrees, c = 3 sqrt(3) cm. Then a and b are:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Angle A = 90 - 60 = 30 degrees. Step 2: tan 60 = c/a gives a = 3 sqrt(3)/sqrt(3) = 3 cm. Step 3: sin 60 = c/b gives b = 3 sqrt(3)/(sqrt(3)/2) = 6 cm.

mcqs.q: In a right triangle with a = sqrt(3) cm and c = sqrt(13) cm (right angle at B), the hypotenuse b is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): b^2 = a^2 + c^2 = 3 + 13 = 16. Step 2: b = 4 cm. (Then angle A = sin^-1(sqrt(3)/4) = 25.66 degrees approx.)

mcqs.q: In a right triangle with angle A = 45 degrees and y (base) = 4 cm, the perpendicular x is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula: tan(angle A) = perpendicular/base, so tan 45 = x/4. Step 2: tan 45 = 1, so x = 4 x 1 = 4 cm.

mcqs.q: A right-angled triangle has legs 12 cm and hypotenuse 20 cm. The third side x is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula (Pythagoras): x^2 = 20^2 - 12^2 = 400 - 144 = 256. Step 2: x = sqrt(256) = 16 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 6.6
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: The angle of elevation of the top of a flag post from a point on the ground level 40 m away from the flag post is 60 degrees. Find the height of the post

Find the height.

Diagram in words: Flag post is the vertical side, the ground is the base; the angle of elevation at the observation point is 60 degrees. Formula: tan(angle of elevation) = height / distance.

Step 1: tan 60 = h/40.

Step 2: h = 40 tan 60 = 40 sqrt(3) = 69.28 m (approx).

Hence the height of the post is about 69.28 m.

Q2: An isosceles triangle has a vertical angle of 120 degrees and a base 10 cm long. Find the length of its altitude

Find the altitude.

The altitude of an isosceles triangle bisects the vertical angle and the base. So we get a right-angled triangle with angle 120/2 = 60 degrees at the top, adjacent side = altitude h, opposite side = half base = 5 cm.

Step 1: Formula: tan 60 = opposite/adjacent = 5/h.

Step 2: h = 5/tan 60 = 5/sqrt(3) = 5 sqrt(3)/3 = 2.89 cm (approx).

Hence the length of the altitude is about 2.89 cm.

Q3: A tree is 72 m high. Find the angle of elevation of its top from a point 100 m away on the ground level

Find the angle of elevation.

Formula: tan(angle of elevation) = height of tree / distance of point.

Step 1: tan theta = 72/100 = 0.72.

Step 2: theta = tan^-1(0.72) = 35.75 degrees (approx).

Hence the angle of elevation is about 35.75 degrees.

Q4: A ladder makes an angle of 60 degrees with the ground and reaches a height of 10 m along the wall. Find the length of the ladder

Find the length of the ladder.

The ladder is the hypotenuse L; the height reached on the wall (10 m) is the side opposite the 60 degree angle. Formula: sin(angle) = opposite/hypotenuse.

Step 1: sin 60 = 10/L.

Step 2: L = 10/sin 60 = 10/(sqrt(3)/2) = 20/sqrt(3) = 20 sqrt(3)/3 = 11.55 m (approx).

Hence the length of the ladder is about 11.55 m.

Q5: A light house tower is 150 m high from the sea level. The angle of depression from the top of the tower to a ship is 60 degrees. Find the distance between the ship and the tower

Find the distance.

The angle of depression from the top of the tower equals the angle of elevation from the ship (alternate angles). Formula: tan(angle) = height / distance.

Step 1: tan 60 = 150/d.

Step 2: d = 150/tan 60 = 150/sqrt(3) = 50 sqrt(3) = 86.60 m (approx).

Hence the distance between the ship and the tower is about 86.60 m.

Q6: Measure of angle of elevation of the top of a pole is 15 degrees from a point on the ground, in walking 100 m towards the pole the measure of angle is found to be 30 degrees. Find the height of the pole

Find the height of the pole.

Let h be the height of the pole and x the distance of the nearer point from the foot of the pole.

Step 1: From the nearer point (angle 30 degrees): tan 30 = h/x, so h = x tan 30 ... (i)

Step 2: From the farther point (angle 15 degrees), distance = x + 100: tan 15 = h/(x + 100), so h = (x + 100) tan 15 ... (ii)

Step 3: Equate (i) and (ii): x tan 30 = (x + 100) tan 15. Using tan 30 = 0.5774 and tan 15 = 0.2679: 0.5774x = 0.2679x + 26.79, so 0.3095x = 26.79 and x = 86.60 m (approx).

Step 4: h = 86.60 x tan 30 = 86.60 x 0.5774 = 50 m (approx).

Hence the height of the pole is about 50 m.

Q7: Find the measure of an angle of elevation of the Sun, if a tower 300 m high casts a shadow 450 m long

Find the angle of elevation of the Sun.

Formula: tan(angle of elevation of the Sun) = height of tower / length of shadow.

Step 1: tan theta = 300/450 = 2/3 = 0.6667.

Step 2: theta = tan^-1(0.6667) = 33.69 degrees (approx).

Hence the angle of elevation of the Sun is about 33.69 degrees.

Q8: Measure of angle of elevation of the top of a cliff is 25 degrees, on walking 100 metres towards the cliff, measure of angle of elevation of the top is 45 degrees. Find the height of the cliff

Find the height of the cliff.

Let h be the height of the cliff and x the distance from the foot of the cliff after walking 100 m towards it.

Step 1: At the nearer point the angle is 45 degrees: tan 45 = h/x, so h = x ... (i)

Step 2: At the farther point (distance x + 100) the angle is 25 degrees: tan 25 = h/(x + 100) ... (ii)

Step 3: From (i) and (ii): x = (x + 100) tan 25 = 0.4663(x + 100). So x - 0.4663x = 46.63, 0.5337x = 46.63, x = 87.37 m (approx).

Step 4: h = x = 87.37 m (approx).

Hence the height of the cliff is about 87.37 m.

Q9: From the top of a hill 300 m high, the measure of the angle of depression of a point on the nearer shore of the river is 70 degrees and measure of the angle of depression of a point, directly across the river is 50 degrees. Find the width of the river. How far is the river from the foot of the hill?

Find the width of the river and its distance from the foot of the hill.

Let the foot of the hill be the reference point; the top of the hill is 300 m above it. The angle of depression to a point equals the angle of elevation from that point to the top.

Step 1: Nearer shore (depression 70 degrees): tan 70 = 300/d1, so d1 = 300/tan 70 = 300/2.7475 = 109.19 m (approx). This is the distance of the nearer shore (the river's near edge) from the foot of the hill.

Step 2: Farther shore, directly across (depression 50 degrees): tan 50 = 300/d2, so d2 = 300/tan 50 = 300/1.1918 = 251.73 m (approx).

Step 3: Width of the river = d2 - d1 = 251.73 - 109.19 = 142.54 m (approx).

Hence the river is about 142.54 m wide, and its nearer shore is about 109.19 m from the foot of the hill.

Q10: A kite has 120 m of string attached to it when at an angle of elevation of 50 degrees. How far is it above the hand holding it? (Assume that the string is stretched)

Find the height of the kite above the hand.

The string is the hypotenuse (120 m); the height of the kite is the side opposite the angle of elevation 50 degrees. Formula: sin(angle) = opposite/hypotenuse.

Step 1: sin 50 = h/120.

Step 2: h = 120 sin 50 = 120 x 0.7660 = 91.93 m (approx).

Hence the kite is about 91.93 m above the hand holding it.

mcqs.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a flag post from a point 40 m away is 60 degrees. The height of the post is:
mcqs.why: Formula: tan(angle of elevation) = height/distance. Step 1: tan 60 = h/40. Step 2: h = 40 tan 60 = 40 sqrt(3) = 69.28 m approximately.

mcqs.q: A tree is 72 m high. The angle of elevation of its top from a point 100 m away is:
mcqs.why: Formula: tan(theta) = height/distance. Step 1: tan theta = 72/100 = 0.72. Step 2: theta = tan^-1(0.72) = 35.75 degrees approximately.

mcqs.q: A ladder makes 60 degrees with the ground and reaches 10 m up a wall. The length of the ladder is:
mcqs.why: The ladder is the hypotenuse and the 10 m height is opposite the 60 degree angle. Formula: sin(angle) = opposite/hypotenuse. Step 1: sin 60 = 10/L. Step 2: L = 10/(sqrt(3)/2) = 20/sqrt(3) = 11.55 m approximately.

mcqs.q: A lighthouse is 150 m high. The angle of depression to a ship is 60 degrees. The distance of the ship from the tower is:
mcqs.why: The angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from the ship. Formula: tan(angle) = height/distance. Step 1: tan 60 = 150/d. Step 2: d = 150/sqrt(3) = 50 sqrt(3) = 86.60 m approximately.

mcqs.q: A tower 300 m high casts a shadow 450 m long. The angle of elevation of the Sun is:
mcqs.why: Formula: tan(theta) = height of tower / length of shadow. Step 1: tan theta = 300/450 = 2/3 = 0.6667. Step 2: theta = tan^-1(0.6667) = 33.69 degrees approximately.

mcqs.q: Walking 100 m towards a pole changes its angle of elevation from 15 degrees to 30 degrees. The height of the pole is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Let h be the height and x the nearer distance: h = x tan 30 and h = (x + 100) tan 15. Step 2: 0.5774x = 0.2679(x + 100) gives x = 86.60 m. Step 3: h = 86.60 x 0.5774 = 50 m approximately.

mcqs.q: A kite has 120 m of string at an angle of elevation of 50 degrees. Its height above the hand is:
mcqs.why: The string is the hypotenuse; the height is the side opposite the 50 degree angle. Formula: sin(angle) = opposite/hypotenuse. Step 1: sin 50 = h/120. Step 2: h = 120 x 0.7660 = 91.93 m approximately.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has vertical angle 120 degrees and base 10 cm. The length of its altitude is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: The altitude bisects the vertical angle and the base, giving a right triangle with angle 60 degrees at the top, opposite side 5 cm and adjacent side h. Step 2: Formula: tan 60 = 5/h. Step 3: h = 5/tan 60 = 5/sqrt(3) = 2.89 cm approximately.

mcqs.q: From a hill 300 m high, angles of depression to the two shores of a river are 70 degrees (nearer) and 50 degrees (farther). The width of the river is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Nearer shore distance d1 = 300/tan 70 = 109.19 m. Step 2: Farther shore distance d2 = 300/tan 50 = 251.73 m. Step 3: Width = d2 - d1 = 251.73 - 109.19 = 142.54 m approximately.

mcqs.q: The angle of depression of a point from the top of a tower is equal to:
options: the angle of elevation of the top of the tower from that point
90 degrees minus the angle of elevation
the angle of elevation of the point from the tower's base
mcqs.why: The line of sight is the same line viewed from opposite ends, and the two angles are alternate interior angles between parallel horizontal lines. Hence the angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the point.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 6
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 (i)

The value of tan^-1 2 in radians is:
(a) pi/2   (b) 3pi/2   (c) 1.11 pi   (d) 1.11
Correct answer: 1.11

Q1 (ii)

In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is 13 units and one of the angles is theta = 30 degrees. The length of the opposite side is:
(a) 6.5 units   (b) 7.5 units   (c) 6 units   (d) 5 units
Correct answer: 6.5 units

Q1 (iii)

A person standing 50 m away from a building sees the top of the building at an angle of elevation of 45 degrees. Height of the building is:
(a) 50 m   (b) 25 m   (c) 35 m   (d) 70 m
Correct answer: 50 m

Q1 (iv)

sec^2 theta - tan^2 theta = _______
(a) sin^2 theta   (b) 1   (c) cos^2 theta   (d) cot^2 theta
Correct answer: 1

Q1 (v)

If sin theta = 3/5 and theta is an acute angle, cos^2 theta = _______
(a) 7/25   (b) 24/25   (c) 16/25   (d) 4/25
Correct answer: 16/25

Q1 (vi)

5pi/24 rad = _______ degrees
(a) 30 degrees   (b) 37.5 degrees   (c) 45 degrees   (d) 52.5 degrees
Correct answer: 37.5 degrees

Q1 (vii)

292.5 degrees = _______ rad
(a) 17pi/6   (b) 17pi/4   (c) 1.6 pi   (d) 1.625 pi
Correct answer: 1.625 pi

Q1 (viii)

Which of the following is a valid identity?
(a) cos(pi/2 - theta) = sin theta   (b) cos(pi/2 - theta) = cos theta   (c) cos(pi/2 - theta) = sec theta   (d) cos(pi/2 - theta) = cosec theta
Correct answer: cos(pi/2 - theta) = sin theta

Q1 (ix)

sin 60 degrees = _______
(a) 1   (b) 1/2   (c) 3   (d) sqrt(3)/2
Correct answer: sqrt(3)/2

Q1 (x)

cos^2 100pi + sin^2 100pi = _______
(a) 1   (b) 2   (c) 3   (d) 4
Correct answer: 1

Q2 (a): Convert the given angles from degrees to radians giving answer in terms of pi

(i) 255 degrees (ii) 75 deg 45 min (iii) 142.5 degrees

Formula: Radians = degrees x pi/180.

(i) 255 degrees = 255pi/180 = 17pi/12 rad.

(ii) 75 degrees 45 minutes = 75 + 45/60 = 75.75 degrees = 75.75pi/180 = 101pi/240 rad.

(iii) 142.5 degrees = 142.5pi/180 = 19pi/24 rad.

Q2 (b): Convert the given angles from radians to degrees giving answer in degrees and minutes

(i) 17pi/24 (ii) 7pi/12 (iii) 11pi/16

Formula: Degrees = radians x 180/pi; the decimal part of the degrees x 60 gives the minutes.

(i) 17pi/24 rad = (17pi/24)(180/pi) = 17 x 7.5 = 127.5 degrees = 127 degrees 30 minutes.

(ii) 7pi/12 rad = (7pi/12)(180/pi) = 7 x 15 = 105 degrees = 105 degrees 0 minutes.

(iii) 11pi/16 rad = (11pi/16)(180/pi) = 11 x 11.25 = 123.75 degrees = 123 degrees 45 minutes.

Q3: Prove the following trigonometric identities

(i) sin theta/(1 - cos theta) = (1 + cos theta)/sin theta (ii) sin theta (cosec theta - sin theta) = 1/sec^2 theta (iii) (cosec theta - sec theta)/(cosec theta + sec theta) = (1 - tan theta)/(1 + tan theta) (iv) tan theta + cot theta = 1/(sin theta cos theta) (v) (cos theta + sin theta)/(cos theta - sin theta) + (cos theta - sin theta)/(cos theta + sin theta) = 2/(1 - 2 sin^2 theta) (vi) (1 + cos theta)/(1 - cos theta) = (cosec theta + cot theta)^2

(i) sin theta/(1 - cos theta) = (1 + cos theta)/sin theta: L.H.S: Multiply numerator and denominator by (1 + cos theta): = sin theta (1 + cos theta) / [(1 - cos theta)(1 + cos theta)] = sin theta (1 + cos theta)/(1 - cos^2 theta) = sin theta (1 + cos theta)/sin^2 theta = (1 + cos theta)/sin theta = R.H.S. Hence proved.

(ii) sin theta (cosec theta - sin theta) = 1/sec^2 theta: L.H.S = sin theta cosec theta - sin^2 theta = 1 - sin^2 theta = cos^2 theta = 1/sec^2 theta = R.H.S. Hence proved.

(iii) (cosec theta - sec theta)/(cosec theta + sec theta) = (1 - tan theta)/(1 + tan theta): Divide numerator and denominator of L.H.S by cosec theta: = (1 - sec theta/cosec theta)/(1 + sec theta/cosec theta). Now sec theta/cosec theta = (1/cos theta)/(1/sin theta) = sin theta/cos theta = tan theta. So L.H.S = (1 - tan theta)/(1 + tan theta) = R.H.S. Hence proved.

(iv) tan theta + cot theta = 1/(sin theta cos theta): L.H.S = sin theta/cos theta + cos theta/sin theta = (sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta)/(sin theta cos theta) = 1/(sin theta cos theta) = R.H.S. Hence proved.

(v) (cos theta + sin theta)/(cos theta - sin theta) + (cos theta - sin theta)/(cos theta + sin theta) = 2/(1 - 2 sin^2 theta): L.H.S: Common denominator (cos theta - sin theta)(cos theta + sin theta) = cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta. Numerator = (cos theta + sin theta)^2 + (cos theta - sin theta)^2 = 2(sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta) = 2. And cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta = (1 - sin^2 theta) - sin^2 theta = 1 - 2 sin^2 theta. So L.H.S = 2/(1 - 2 sin^2 theta) = R.H.S. Hence proved.

(vi) (1 + cos theta)/(1 - cos theta) = (cosec theta + cot theta)^2: R.H.S = (1/sin theta + cos theta/sin theta)^2 = [(1 + cos theta)/sin theta]^2 = (1 + cos theta)^2/sin^2 theta = (1 + cos theta)^2/(1 - cos^2 theta) = (1 + cos theta)^2/[(1 - cos theta)(1 + cos theta)] = (1 + cos theta)/(1 - cos theta) = L.H.S. Hence proved.

Q4: If tan theta = 3/sqrt(2) then find the remaining trigonometric ratios when theta lies in first quadrant

Find the remaining ratios.

Given tan theta = 3/sqrt(2), theta in the first quadrant.

Step 1: Formula: sec^2 theta = 1 + tan^2 theta = 1 + 9/2 = 11/2, so sec theta = sqrt(11/2) = sqrt(22)/2.

Step 2: cos theta = 1/sec theta = sqrt(2/11) = sqrt(22)/11.

Step 3: sin theta = tan theta x cos theta = (3/sqrt(2)) x (sqrt(2)/sqrt(11)) = 3/sqrt(11) = 3 sqrt(11)/11.

Step 4: cot theta = 1/tan theta = sqrt(2)/3; cosec theta = 1/sin theta = sqrt(11)/3.

Hence: sin theta = 3/sqrt(11), cos theta = sqrt(2/11), cot theta = sqrt(2)/3, sec theta = sqrt(22)/2, cosec theta = sqrt(11)/3.

Q5: From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation to the top of a 30 m high building is 28 degrees. How far is the point from the base of the building?

Find the distance.

Formula: tan(angle of elevation) = height / distance.

Step 1: tan 28 = 30/d.

Step 2: d = 30/tan 28 = 30/0.5317 = 56.42 m (approx).

Hence the point is about 56.42 m from the base of the building.

Q6: A ladder leaning against a wall forms an angle of 65 degrees with the ground. If the ladder is 10 m long, how high does it reach on the wall?

Find the height reached.

The ladder is the hypotenuse (10 m); the height reached is the side opposite the 65 degree angle. Formula: sin(angle) = opposite/hypotenuse.

Step 1: sin 65 = h/10.

Step 2: h = 10 sin 65 = 10 x 0.9063 = 9.06 m (approx).

Hence the ladder reaches about 9.06 m up the wall.

mcqs.q: The value of tan^-1 (2) in radians is:
mcqs.why: tan^-1 (2) means the angle whose tangent is 2. From tables/calculator it is about 63.43 degrees, which in radians is 63.43 x pi/180 = 1.11 rad approximately (not 1.11 pi).

mcqs.q: In a right triangle the hypotenuse is 13 units and one angle is theta = 30 degrees. The length of the side opposite theta is:
mcqs.why: Formula: sin(theta) = opposite/hypotenuse. Step 1: sin 30 = opposite/13. Step 2: opposite = 13 x (1/2) = 6.5 units.

mcqs.q: A person 50 m from a building sees its top at an angle of elevation of 45 degrees. The height of the building is:
mcqs.why: Formula: tan(angle of elevation) = height/distance. Step 1: tan 45 = h/50. Step 2: tan 45 = 1, so h = 50 m.

mcqs.q: sec^2 theta - tan^2 theta =
mcqs.why: Step 1: Divide sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1 by cos^2 theta: tan^2 theta + 1 = sec^2 theta. Step 2: Rearranged: sec^2 theta - tan^2 theta = 1.

mcqs.q: If sin theta = 3/5 and theta is acute, then cos^2 theta =
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula: cos^2 theta = 1 - sin^2 theta = 1 - 9/25. Step 2: = 16/25 (so cos theta = 4/5 for an acute angle).

mcqs.q: 5pi/24 radians in degrees is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Degrees = radians x (180/pi). Step: (5pi/24) x (180/pi) = 5 x 7.5 = 37.5 degrees.

mcqs.q: 292.5 degrees in radians is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Radians = degrees x (pi/180). Step: 292.5 x pi/180 = (292.5/180) pi = 1.625 pi rad (i.e. 13pi/8).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a valid identity?
mcqs.why: Complementary-angle formula: cos(90 degrees - theta) = sin theta, and pi/2 rad = 90 degrees. So cos(pi/2 - theta) = sin theta is the valid identity.

mcqs.q: sin 60 degrees =
mcqs.why: From the 30-60-90 triangle (sides 1, sqrt(3), 2): sin 60 = opposite/hypotenuse = sqrt(3)/2.
The identity sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1 holds for EVERY angle A. With A = 100pi, cos^2 (100pi) + sin^2 (100pi) = 1.

mcqs.q: 255 degrees in radians (in terms of pi) is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Radians = degrees x (pi/180). Step: 255pi/180 simplifies (divide by 15) to 17pi/12 rad.

mcqs.q: 17pi/24 radians in degrees and minutes is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Degrees = radians x (180/pi). Step 1: (17pi/24)(180/pi) = 17 x 7.5 = 127.5 degrees. Step 2: 0.5 degree = 30 minutes, so 127 degrees 30 minutes.

mcqs.q: tan theta + cot theta is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step: tan + cot = sin/cos + cos/sin = (sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta)/(sin theta cos theta) = 1/(sin theta cos theta), using sin^2 + cos^2 = 1.

mcqs.q: If tan theta = 3/sqrt(2) (first quadrant), then sin theta is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula: sec^2 theta = 1 + tan^2 theta = 1 + 9/2 = 11/2, so cos theta = sqrt(2/11). Step 2: sin theta = tan theta x cos theta = (3/sqrt(2))(sqrt(2)/sqrt(11)) = 3/sqrt(11).

mcqs.q: From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation to the top of a 30 m building is 28 degrees. The distance of the point from the base is:
mcqs.why: Formula: tan(angle of elevation) = height/distance. Step 1: tan 28 = 30/d. Step 2: d = 30/tan 28 = 30/0.5317 = 56.42 m approximately.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: Describe the location in the plane of the point P(x, y), for which

(i) x > 0 (ii) x > 0 and y > 0 (iii) x = 0 (iv) y = 0 (v) x > 0 and y <= 0 (vi) y = 0, x = 0 (vii) x = y (viii) x >= 3 (ix) y > 0 (x) x and y have opposite signs

(i) x > 0: All points to the right of the y-axis (the right half-plane, quadrants I and IV and the positive x-axis side).

(ii) x > 0 and y > 0: The first quadrant.

(iii) x = 0: All points on the y-axis.

(iv) y = 0: All points on the x-axis.

(v) x > 0 and y <= 0: The fourth quadrant together with the points of the positive x-axis (y = 0, x > 0).

(vi) y = 0 and x = 0: The single point (0, 0), the origin.

(vii) x = y: All points whose abscissa equals the ordinate — the straight line through the origin bisecting the first and third quadrants at 45 degrees to the axes.

(viii) x >= 3: All points on the vertical line x = 3 and to its right.

(ix) y > 0: The upper half-plane (first and second quadrants, above the x-axis).

(x) x and y have opposite signs: The second quadrant (x < 0, y > 0) and the fourth quadrant (x > 0, y < 0).

Q2: Find the distance between the points

(i) A(6, 7), B(0, -2) (ii) C(-5, -2), D(3, 2) (iii) L(0, 3), M(-2, -4) (iv) P(-8, -7), Q(0, 0)

Formula: Distance d = sqrt[(x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2].

(i) A(6, 7), B(0, -2): d = sqrt[(0 - 6)^2 + (-2 - 7)^2] = sqrt[36 + 81] = sqrt(117) = 3 sqrt(13) = 10.82 units (approx).

(ii) C(-5, -2), D(3, 2): d = sqrt[(3 + 5)^2 + (2 + 2)^2] = sqrt[64 + 16] = sqrt(80) = 4 sqrt(5) = 8.94 units (approx).

(iii) L(0, 3), M(-2, -4): d = sqrt[(-2 - 0)^2 + (-4 - 3)^2] = sqrt[4 + 49] = sqrt(53) = 7.28 units (approx).
