(vii) The class having 15 as its class frequency is 44-48; its lower limit is 44.

(viii) Students having scores between 24 and 43 = frequencies of 24-28, 29-33, 34-38, 39-43 = 3 + 6 + 12 + 23 = 44 students.

Q2: For a school staff, the following expenditures (rupees in hundred) are required for the repair of chairs. Prepare a frequency distribution by tally bar method by taking number of classes 8, also write down what are the frequencies of the last three classes?

Prepare the frequency distribution.

Data (30 values): 145, 152, 153, 156, 158, 160, 146, 152, 155, 159, 161, 163, 165, 147, 148, 151, 154, 156, 158, 160, 144, 167, 151, 150, 152, 149, 145, 153, 152, 155 (rupees in hundred).

Step 1: Range: Formula: Range = greatest value - smallest value = 167 - 144 = 23.

Step 2: Size of class: Formula: Size = Range / Number of classes = 23/8 = 2.875, taken as 3.

Step 3: Frequency distribution (tally bar method — each value is ticked in its class; tallies counted to give f):
Class 144-146: f = 4
Class 147-149: f = 3
Class 150-152: f = 7
Class 153-155: f = 5
Class 156-158: f = 4
Class 159-161: f = 4
Class 162-164: f = 1
Class 165-167: f = 2
Total = 30 ✓.

The frequencies of the last three classes are: 159-161: 4; 162-164: 1; 165-167: 2.

Q3: Given below are the weights in kg of 30 students of a high school. Taking 6 as the number of classes, prepare a frequency table and construct a frequency polygon

Prepare the table and the polygon.

Data (30 weights): 30, 33, 24, 21, 15, 39, 37, 44, 42, 33, 33, 28, 29, 32, 31, 28, 26, 32, 34, 35, 38, 36, 41, 30, 35, 41, 23, 26, 18, 34.

Step 1: Range = 44 - 15 = 29. Size of class = 29/6 = 4.83, taken as 5.

Step 2: Frequency table:
Class 15-19: f = 2
Class 20-24: f = 3
Class 25-29: f = 5
Class 30-34: f = 10
Class 35-39: f = 6
Class 40-44: f = 4
Total = 30 ✓.

Step 3: Frequency polygon (in words): Midpoints of the classes are 17, 22, 27, 32, 37, 42. Plot the points (17, 2), (22, 3), (27, 5), (32, 10), (37, 6), (42, 4) and join them in order with straight line segments; extend the line at both ends down to the x-axis at the neighbouring midpoints 12 and 47 (frequency 0). The polygon rises to its peak above 32 kg and then falls.

Q4: A group of Grade-10 students obtained marks out of 100 in English test. Classify the data into a frequency distribution by (direct method) taking 5 as the number of classes. Also find the class limit with least class frequency and construct histogram for the data

Classify the data, find the least-frequency class and construct the histogram.

Data (32 marks): 58, 59, 58, 33, 40, 58, 45, 46, 43, 45, 45, 50, 52, 49, 50, 57, 52, 55, 49, 50, 62, 49, 48, 44, 42, 47, 46, 47, 46, 53, 40, 44.

Step 1: Range = 62 - 33 = 29. Size of class = 29/5 = 5.8, taken as 6.

Step 2: Frequency distribution (direct method):
Class 33-38: f = 1
Class 39-44: f = 6
Class 45-50: f = 15
Class 51-56: f = 4
Class 57-62: f = 6
Total = 32 ✓.

Step 3: The class limit with the least class frequency is 33-38 (only 1 student).

Step 4: Histogram (in words): Class boundaries are 32.5-38.5, 38.5-44.5, 44.5-50.5, 50.5-56.5, 56.5-62.5. Draw touching rectangles on these intervals with heights 1, 6, 15, 4, 6 respectively; the tallest bar is over 44.5-50.5.

Q5: From the table given below. Draw a frequency polygon on histogram for the given frequency distribution. Weight (kg): 10-14 (06), 15-19 (17), 20-24 (23), 25-29 (30), 30-34 (22), 35-39 (13)

Draw the frequency polygon on the histogram.

Classes and frequencies: 10-14 (6), 15-19 (17), 20-24 (23), 25-29 (30), 30-34 (22), 35-39 (13).

Step 1: Class boundaries: 9.5-14.5, 14.5-19.5, 19.5-24.5, 24.5-29.5, 29.5-34.5, 34.5-39.5. The histogram (in words) is the row of touching rectangles on these intervals with heights 6, 17, 23, 30, 22, 13.

Step 2: Midpoints: 12, 17, 22, 27, 32, 37. Mark the points (12, 6), (17, 17), (22, 23), (27, 30), (32, 22), (37, 13) at the top-centre of each rectangle.

Step 3: Join the points in order by straight segments and extend both ends to the x-axis at midpoints 7 and 42. This is the frequency polygon on the histogram; it peaks above the class 25-29.

Q6: The following data shows the number of heads in an experiment of 50 sets of tossing a coin 5 times. Make a discrete frequency distribution from the information. 3, 3, 4, 0, 5, 4, 3, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 0, 3, 2, 4, 4, 0, 0, 0, 5, 5, 3, 2, 1, 4, 3, 2, 5, 3, 2, 1, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 4, 3, 2, 2, 4

Make the discrete frequency distribution.

Counting each value in the 50 sets gives the discrete frequency distribution:
Number of heads 0: f = 5
Number of heads 1: f = 7
Number of heads 2: f = 9
Number of heads 3: f = 14
Number of heads 4: f = 9
Number of heads 5: f = 6
Total = 5 + 7 + 9 + 14 + 9 + 6 = 50 ✓.

So 3 heads occurred most often (14 times).

Q7: The marks obtained by the students of Grade-10 in mathematics test were grouped into the following frequency distribution. Marks: 35-37 (2), 38-44 (12), 45-54 (16), 55-61 (13), 62-67 (9), 68-72 (3). Draw a histogram for the above distribution

Draw the histogram.

The class widths are unequal, so the rectangle heights must be adjusted: Formula: Adjusted frequency (height) = frequency / width of class, using class boundaries.

Step 1: Class boundaries and widths: 34.5-37.5 (width 3), 37.5-44.5 (width 7), 44.5-54.5 (width 10), 54.5-61.5 (width 7), 61.5-67.5 (width 6), 67.5-72.5 (width 5).

Step 2: Heights: 2/3 = 0.67; 12/7 = 1.71; 16/10 = 1.6; 13/7 = 1.86; 9/6 = 1.5; 3/5 = 0.6.

Step 3: Histogram (in words): Draw touching rectangles on the six boundary intervals with these heights: 0.67, 1.71, 1.6, 1.86, 1.5, 0.6. The tallest rectangle is over 54.5-61.5 and the shortest over 67.5-72.5; areas of the rectangles are proportional to the frequencies.

Q8: Make a frequency polygon on histogram for the following grouped data: Class limits 5-8 (2), 8-12 (12), 12-20 (25), 20-25 (32), 25-27 (14), 27-32 (5)

Make the frequency polygon on the histogram.

The classes are continuous (5-8, 8-12, ...) but of unequal width, so use adjusted frequencies: Formula: Height = f / width.

Step 1: Widths: 3, 4, 8, 5, 2, 5. Adjusted heights: 2/3 = 0.67; 12/4 = 3; 25/8 = 3.125; 32/5 = 6.4; 14/2 = 7; 5/5 = 1.

Step 2: Histogram (in words): rectangles on 5-8, 8-12, 12-20, 20-25, 25-27, 27-32 with heights 0.67, 3, 3.125, 6.4, 7, 1. The narrow class 25-27 gives the tallest rectangle.

Step 3: Midpoints: 6.5, 10, 16, 22.5, 26, 29.5. Mark (6.5, 0.67), (10, 3), (16, 3.125), (22.5, 6.4), (26, 7), (29.5, 1) at the top-centres and join them in order by straight segments, extending the ends to the x-axis — this is the frequency polygon on the histogram.

mcqs.why: Formula: Midpoint = (lower limit + upper limit)/2. Step: (34 + 38)/2 = 72/2 = 36.

mcqs.q: In the same distribution, the size of each class is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Class size = lower limit of a class - lower limit of the previous class. Step: 29 - 24 = 5 (the same gap holds between every pair of consecutive classes).

mcqs.q: In the same distribution, the number of students with scores between 24 and 43 is:
mcqs.why: Add the frequencies of the classes 24-28, 29-33, 34-38 and 39-43. Step: 3 + 6 + 12 + 23 = 44 students. (The total frequency of all classes is 65.)

mcqs.q: For data with greatest value 167 and smallest value 144, split into 8 classes, the class size is taken as:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula: Range = greatest - smallest = 167 - 144 = 23. Step 2: Formula: Size = Range / number of classes = 23/8 = 2.875. Step 3: Round UP to a convenient value: 3, giving classes 144-146, 147-149, and so on.

mcqs.q: In the coin-toss experiment (50 sets of 5 tosses), the number of heads that occurred most often was:
mcqs.why: Counting the 50 results: 0 heads: 5, 1: 7, 2: 9, 3: 14, 4: 9, 5: 6 (total 50). The largest frequency, 14, belongs to 3 heads.

mcqs.q: For a frequency polygon, the points are plotted at:
options: (midpoint of each class, frequency of the class)
mcqs.why: A frequency polygon joins the points (class midpoint, class frequency) with straight segments, extended to the x-axis at the neighbouring midpoints with frequency 0. Midpoints here are e.g. 17, 22, 27, 32, 37, 42 for classes 15-19 up to 40-44.

mcqs.q: When class widths are UNEQUAL, the height of a histogram rectangle is:
options: the adjusted frequency = frequency / width of the class
mcqs.why: With unequal widths the AREA of each rectangle must be proportional to the frequency. Formula: height = f / width. E.g. the class 45-54 (width 10, f = 16) gets height 16/10 = 1.6, while 35-37 (width 3, f = 2) gets 2/3 = 0.67.

mcqs.q: For classes 5-8 (2), 8-12 (12), 12-20 (25), the adjusted heights are:
mcqs.why: Formula: height = f / width. Step: widths are 3, 4, 8. Heights: 2/3 = 0.67; 12/4 = 3; 25/8 = 3.125.

mcqs.q: The class boundaries of the class 10-14 (in a distribution with classes 10-14, 15-19, ...) are:
mcqs.why: The gap between consecutive classes is 15 - 14 = 1, so half the gap (0.5) is subtracted from the lower limit and added to the upper limit: 10 - 0.5 = 9.5 and 14 + 0.5 = 14.5.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: Find the arithmetic mean in each of the following

(i) 4, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 25, 28, 30 (ii) 12, 18 19, 0, -19, -18, -12 (iii) 6.5, 11, 12.3, 9, 8.1, 16, 18, 20.5, 25 (iv) 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 20, 22

Formula: Arithmetic Mean = (sum of values) / (number of values) = Sum(x)/n.

(i) Sum = 4 + 6 + 10 + 12 + 15 + 20 + 25 + 28 + 30 = 150; n = 9. Mean = 150/9 = 16.67.

(ii) Sum = 12 + 18 + 19 + 0 - 19 - 18 - 12 = 0; n = 7. Mean = 0/7 = 0.

(iii) Sum = 6.5 + 11 + 12.3 + 9 + 8.1 + 16 + 18 + 20.5 + 25 = 126.4; n = 9. Mean = 126.4/9 = 14.04 (approx).

(iv) Sum = 8 + 10 + 12 + 14 + 16 + 20 + 22 = 102; n = 7. Mean = 102/7 = 14.57 (approx).

Q2: Following are the heights in (inches) of 12 students. Find the median height. 55, 53, 54, 58, 60, 61, 62, 56, 57, 52, 51, 63

Find the median height.

Step 1: Arrange in ascending order: 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 60, 61, 62, 63.

Step 2: n = 12 is even. Formula: Median = (1/2)[(n/2)th observation + (n/2 + 1)th observation] = (1/2)[6th + 7th] = (1/2)(56 + 57) = 113/2 = 56.5.

Hence the median height is 56.5 inches.

Q3: Following are the earnings (in Rs.) of ten workers: 88, 70, 72, 125, 115, 95, 81, 90, 95, 90. Calculate (i) Arithmetic Mean (ii) Median (iii) Mode

Calculate mean, median and mode.

Data: 88, 70, 72, 125, 115, 95, 81, 90, 95, 90 (Rs.).

(i) Arithmetic Mean: Formula: Mean = Sum(x)/n = (88 + 70 + 72 + 125 + 115 + 95 + 81 + 90 + 95 + 90)/10 = 921/10 = Rs. 92.1.

(ii) Median: Arrange: 70, 72, 81, 88, 90, 90, 95, 95, 115, 125. n = 10, so Median = (1/2)(5th + 6th) = (1/2)(90 + 90) = Rs. 90.

(iii) Mode: 90 occurs twice and 95 also occurs twice; every other value occurs once. So the data is bimodal: Mode = Rs. 90 and Rs. 95.

Q4: The Marks obtained by the students in the subject of English are given below. Marks obtained: 15-19 (9), 20-24 (18), 25-29 (35), 30-34 (17), 35-39 (5). Find: (i) Arithmetic mean of their marks by direct and short formula. (ii) Median of their marks

Find the mean (both methods) and the median.

Classes (boundaries 14.5-19.5, ..., 34.5-39.5), midpoints x: 17, 22, 27, 32, 37; f: 9, 18, 35, 17, 5; Sum(f) = 84.

(i) Direct method: fx: 17x9 = 153; 22x18 = 396; 27x35 = 945; 32x17 = 544; 37x5 = 185. Sum(fx) = 2223. Formula: Mean = Sum(fx)/Sum(f) = 2223/84 = 26.46 marks.

Short formula: Take A = 27. D = x - A: -10, -5, 0, 5, 10. fD: -90, -90, 0, 85, 50; Sum(fD) = -45. Formula: Mean = A + Sum(fD)/Sum(f) = 27 + (-45)/84 = 27 - 0.54 = 26.46 marks ✓ (same result).

(ii) Median: Cumulative frequencies: 9, 27, 62, 79, 84. n/2 = 42, which lies in the class 24.5-29.5 (c.f. 62). So l = 24.5, h = 5, f = 35, c = 27. Formula: Median = l + (h/f)(n/2 - c) = 24.5 + (5/35)(42 - 27) = 24.5 + (5/35)(15) = 24.5 + 2.14 = 26.64 marks.

Q5: Given below is a frequency distribution. Class Interval: 5-9 (1), 10-14 (8), 15-19 (18), 20-24 (11), 25-29 (2). Find the mode of the frequency distribution

Find the mode.

The modal class is the class with the highest frequency: 15-19 with f = 18. Its class boundaries are 14.5-19.5, so l = 14.5, h = 5, fm = 18, f1 = 8 (preceding class), f2 = 11 (following class).

Formula: Mode = l + [(fm - f1) / ((fm - f1) + (fm - f2))] x h
= 14.5 + [(18 - 8) / ((18 - 8) + (18 - 11))] x 5
= 14.5 + [10 / (10 + 7)] x 5
= 14.5 + (10/17) x 5
= 14.5 + 2.94
= 17.44 (approx).

Q6: Ten boys work on a petrol pump station. They get weekly wages as follows: Wages (in Rs.) 4250, 4350, 4400, 4250, 4350, 4410, 4500, 4300, 4500, 4390. Find the arithmetic mean by short formula, median and mode of their wages

Find mean, median and mode.

Wages: 4250, 4350, 4400, 4250, 4350, 4410, 4500, 4300, 4500, 4390.

Arithmetic mean by short formula: Take A = 4350. D = x - A: -100, 0, 50, -100, 0, 60, 150, -50, 150, 40. Sum(D) = 200. Formula: Mean = A + Sum(D)/n = 4350 + 200/10 = 4350 + 20 = Rs. 4370. (Check by direct method: sum of wages = 43,700; 43700/10 = 4370 ✓.)

Median: Arrange: 4250, 4250, 4300, 4350, 4350, 4390, 4400, 4410, 4500, 4500. Median = (1/2)(5th + 6th) = (1/2)(4350 + 4390) = Rs. 4370.

Mode: 4250, 4350 and 4500 each occur twice, all others once — the wages have three modes: Rs. 4250, Rs. 4350 and Rs. 4500 (trimodal).

Q7: The arithmetic mean of 45 numbers is 80. Find their sum

Find the sum.

Formula: Sum = Mean x n (from Mean = Sum/n).

Step 1: Sum = 80 x 45 = 3600.

Hence the sum of the 45 numbers is 3600.

Q8: Five numbers are 1, 4, 0, 7, 9. Find their mean, median and mode

Find mean, median and mode.

Data: 1, 4, 0, 7, 9.

Mean: Formula: Mean = Sum(x)/n = (1 + 4 + 0 + 7 + 9)/5 = 21/5 = 4.2.

Median: Arrange: 0, 1, 4, 7, 9. n = 5 is odd, so Median = ((n + 1)/2)th observation = 3rd observation = 4.

Mode: Every value occurs exactly once, so the data has no mode.

Q9: A set of data contains the values as 148, 145, 160, 157, 156, 160. Show that Mode > Median > Mean

Show the inequality.

Data: 148, 145, 160, 157, 156, 160.

Mean: Sum = 148 + 145 + 160 + 157 + 156 + 160 = 926. Mean = 926/6 = 154.33.

Median: Arrange: 145, 148, 156, 157, 160, 160. Median = (1/2)(3rd + 4th) = (1/2)(156 + 157) = 156.5.

Mode: 160 occurs twice, more than any other value, so Mode = 160.

Comparison: Mode (160) > Median (156.5) > Mean (154.33). Hence Mode > Median > Mean, as required.

Q10: The monthly attendance of 10 students for their lunch in the hostel is recorded as: 21, 15, 16, 18, 14, 17, 15, 12, 13, 11. Find the median and mode of the attendance. Also find the mean if D = A - 20

Find median, mode and mean.

Data: 21, 15, 16, 18, 14, 17, 15, 12, 13, 11.

Median: Arrange: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 21. Median = (1/2)(5th + 6th) = (1/2)(15 + 15) = 15.

Mode: 15 occurs twice, more than any other value, so Mode = 15.

Mean (using D = x - A with A = 20): D values: 1, -5, -4, -2, -6, -3, -5, -8, -7, -9. Sum(D) = -48. Formula: Mean = A + Sum(D)/n = 20 + (-48)/10 = 20 - 4.8 = 15.2.

Q11: On a prize distribution day, 50 students brought pocket money as under: Rupees 5-10 (12), 10-15 (9), 15-20 (18), 20-25 (7), 25-30 (4). (i) Find the median and mode of the above data. (ii) Find the arithmetic mean of the data given above using coding method

Find median, mode and mean.

n = 50. Cumulative frequencies: 12, 21, 39, 46, 50.

(i) Median: n/2 = 25 lies in the class 15-20 (c.f. 39). l = 15, h = 5, f = 18, c = 21. Formula: Median = l + (h/f)(n/2 - c) = 15 + (5/18)(25 - 21) = 15 + 20/18 = 15 + 1.11 = Rs. 16.11.

Mode: Modal class is 15-20 (highest f = 18). l = 15, fm = 18, f1 = 9, f2 = 7, h = 5. Formula: Mode = l + [(fm - f1)/((fm - f1) + (fm - f2))] x h = 15 + [(9)/(9 + 11)] x 5 = 15 + (9/20) x 5 = 15 + 2.25 = Rs. 17.25.

(ii) Mean by coding method: Midpoints x: 7.5, 12.5, 17.5, 22.5, 27.5. Take A = 17.5 and h = 5; U = (x - A)/h: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. fU: 12x(-2) = -24; 9x(-1) = -9; 18x0 = 0; 7x1 = 7; 4x2 = 8. Sum(fU) = -18. Formula: Mean = A + h x Sum(fU)/Sum(f) = 17.5 + 5 x (-18/50) = 17.5 - 1.8 = Rs. 15.7. (Check by direct method: Sum(fx) = 785; 785/50 = 15.7 ✓.)

Q12: The arithmetic mean of the ages of 20 boys is 13 years, 4 months and 5 days. Find the sum of their ages. If one of the boys is of age exactly 15 years. What is the average age of the remaining boys?

Find the sum and the new average.

Step 1: Convert the mean age to days using 1 year = 365 days and 1 month = 30 days: 13 years 4 months 5 days = 13x365 + 4x30 + 5 = 4745 + 120 + 5 = 4870 days.

Step 2: Sum of the ages of 20 boys = 20 x 4870 = 97,400 days.

Step 3: The boy who leaves is exactly 15 years old = 15 x 365 = 5475 days. Sum for the remaining 19 boys = 97,400 - 5,475 = 91,925 days.

Step 4: Average of the remaining boys = 91,925/19 = 4838.2 days (approx).

Step 5: Convert back: 4838.2 days = 13 years (4745 days) with 93.2 days left = 3 months (90 days) with about 3 days left.

Hence the average age of the remaining boys is about 13 years, 3 months and 3 days.

Q13: Calculate the arithmetic mean from the following information: (i) If D = X - 140, Sum(D) = 500 and n = 10 (ii) If U = (x - 130)/6, Sum(U) = -150 and n = 15 (iii) If D = x - 25, Sum(fD) = 300 and Sum(f) = 20 (vi) If U = (x - 120)/5, Sum(fU) = 60 and Sum(f) = 100

Calculate the four means.

Formula (short/coding method): Mean = A + Sum(D)/n for deviations D = x - A, and Mean = A + h x Sum(U)/n for coded values U = (x - A)/h.

(i) D = X - 140, so A = 140. Mean = 140 + 500/10 = 140 + 50 = 190.

(ii) U = (x - 130)/6, so A = 130, h = 6. Mean = 130 + 6 x (-150/15) = 130 + 6 x (-10) = 130 - 60 = 70.

(iii) D = x - 25, so A = 25. Mean = 25 + Sum(fD)/Sum(f) = 25 + 300/20 = 25 + 15 = 40.

(vi) U = (x - 120)/5, so A = 120, h = 5. Mean = 120 + 5 x (60/100) = 120 + 5 x 0.6 = 120 + 3 = 123.

Note: In the book this question's parts are numbered (i), (ii), (iii), (vi) — the labels (iv) and (v) are missing in the printed book. Flagged in the manifest.

Q14: The three children Haris, Maham and Minal made the following scores in a game. Haris scores: 50, 55, 70, 85, 90. Maham scores: 75, 60, 60, 45, 53. Minal scores: 80, 77, 66, 42, 48. It is decided that the candidate who gets the highest average score will be awarded rupees 1000. Who will get the awarded amount?

Find who gets the award.

Formula: Average = (sum of the 5 scores)/5.

Haris: (50 + 55 + 70 + 85 + 90)/5 = 350/5 = 70.

Maham: (75 + 60 + 60 + 45 + 53)/5 = 293/5 = 58.6.

Minal: (80 + 77 + 66 + 42 + 48)/5 = 313/5 = 62.6.

Haris has the highest average score (70), so Haris will get the awarded amount of rupees 1000.

Q15: Given below is a frequency distribution derived by making a substitution as D = X - 20. Calculate the arithmetic mean. D: -6 (1), -4 (3), -2 (6), 0 (20), 2 (26), 4 (12), 6 (2)

Calculate the mean.

Here the deviations are already given: D = X - 20, so the assumed mean is A = 20.

Step 1: Sum(f) = 1 + 3 + 6 + 20 + 26 + 12 + 2 = 70.

Step 2: fD values: 1x(-6) = -6; 3x(-4) = -12; 6x(-2) = -12; 20x0 = 0; 26x2 = 52; 12x4 = 48; 2x6 = 12. Sum(fD) = -6 - 12 - 12 + 0 + 52 + 48 + 12 = 82.

Step 3: Formula: Mean = A + Sum(fD)/Sum(f) = 20 + 82/70 = 20 + 1.17 = 21.17 (approx).

Q16: Being partners Hafsa and Fatima took part in a quiz programme. They made the following number of points 45, 51, 58, 61, 74, 48, 46 and 50. Compute the average number of points using deviation D = x - 58

Compute the average.

Points: 45, 51, 58, 61, 74, 48, 46, 50 (8 values). Use deviations D = x - 58 (so A = 58).

Step 1: D values: 45 - 58 = -13; 51 - 58 = -7; 58 - 58 = 0; 61 - 58 = 3; 74 - 58 = 16; 48 - 58 = -10; 46 - 58 = -12; 50 - 58 = -8.

Step 2: Sum(D) = -13 - 7 + 0 + 3 + 16 - 10 - 12 - 8 = -31.

Step 3: Formula: Mean = A + Sum(D)/n = 58 + (-31)/8 = 58 - 3.875 = 54.125.

Hence the average number of points is 54.125 (about 54.13).

Q17: A person purchased the following food items: Rice 10 kg at Rs. 96 per kg; Flour 12 kg at Rs. 48; Ghee 4 kg at Rs. 190; Sugar 3 kg at Rs. 49; Mutton 2 kg at Rs. 650. What is the weighted mean of cost of food items per kg?

Find the weighted mean cost per kg.

The weighted mean cost per kg uses the quantities as weights and the costs per kg as the values. Formula: Weighted mean = Sum(WX)/Sum(W).

Step 1: WX values: Rice: 10 x 96 = 960. Flour: 12 x 48 = 576. Ghee: 4 x 190 = 760. Sugar: 3 x 49 = 147. Mutton: 2 x 650 = 1300. Sum(WX) = 960 + 576 + 760 + 147 + 1300 = 3743.

Step 2: Sum(W) = 10 + 12 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 31 kg.

Step 3: Weighted mean = 3743/31 = Rs. 120.74 per kg (approx).

Q18: For the following data, find the weighted mean. Washing Machine: quantity 5, cost 35 (thousands); Heater: 3, 5; Stove: 2, 13; Dispenser: 6, 18

Find the weighted mean.

Quantities are the weights; costs (in thousands of rupees) are the values. Formula: Weighted mean = Sum(WX)/Sum(W).

Step 1: WX values: Washing Machine: 5 x 35 = 175. Heater: 3 x 5 = 15. Stove: 2 x 13 = 26. Dispenser: 6 x 18 = 108. Sum(WX) = 175 + 15 + 26 + 108 = 324.

Step 2: Sum(W) = 5 + 3 + 2 + 6 = 16.

Step 3: Weighted mean = 324/16 = 20.25, i.e. Rs. 20.25 thousand = Rs. 20,250 per item.

Q19: A company is planning its next year marketing budget across five years: yearly budgets (in million) are: 5, 7, 8, 6, 7. Find the average budget for the next year

Find the average budget.

Formula: Average budget = (sum of yearly budgets)/(number of years).

Step 1: Sum = 5 + 7 + 8 + 6 + 7 = 33 million.

Step 2: Average = 33/5 = 6.6 million.

Hence the average budget — and the expected budget for the next year on this basis — is Rs. 6.6 million.

Q20: Ahmad obtained the following marks in a certain examination. Find the weighted mean if weights 5, 4, 2, 3, 2, 4 respectively are allotted to the subjects. Urdu 78, English 65, Science 80, Math 90, Islamiyat 85, Computer 72

Find the weighted mean.

Subjects, marks and weights: Urdu 78 (weight 5), English 65 (4), Science 80 (2), Math 90 (3), Islamiyat 85 (2), Computer 72 (4).

Formula: Weighted mean = Sum(WX)/Sum(W).

Step 1: WX values: 5x78 = 390; 4x65 = 260; 2x80 = 160; 3x90 = 270; 2x85 = 170; 4x72 = 288. Sum(WX) = 390 + 260 + 160 + 270 + 170 + 288 = 1538.

Step 2: Sum(W) = 5 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 4 = 20.

Step 3: Weighted mean = 1538/20 = 76.9 marks.

mcqs.q: The arithmetic mean of 4, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 25, 28, 30 is:

mcqs.why: Formula: Mean = Sum(x)/n. Step: Sum = 12 + 18 + 19 + 0 - 19 - 18 - 12 = 0 (the positives cancel the negatives), so Mean = 0/7 = 0.

mcqs.q: The median height of 12 students with heights 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 60, 61, 62, 63 inches (arranged) is:
mcqs.why: n = 12 is even. Formula: Median = (1/2)[(n/2)th + (n/2 + 1)th observations] = (1/2)(6th + 7th) = (1/2)(56 + 57) = 56.5 inches.

mcqs.q: Workers earn (Rs.) 88, 70, 72, 125, 115, 95, 81, 90, 95, 90. Their mean, median and modes are:
options: mean Rs. 92.1, median Rs. 95, mode Rs. 90 only
mean Rs. 92.1, median Rs. 90, modes Rs. 90 and Rs. 95 (bimodal)
mean Rs. 90, median Rs. 90, mode Rs. 95 only
mean Rs. 921, median Rs. 90, no mode
mcqs.why: Step 1: Mean = 921/10 = Rs. 92.1. Step 2: Arranged: 70, 72, 81, 88, 90, 90, 95, 95, 115, 125; median = (1/2)(5th + 6th) = (1/2)(90 + 90) = Rs. 90. Step 3: 90 and 95 each occur twice — two modes (bimodal).

mcqs.q: For the numbers 1, 4, 0, 7, 9, the mean, median and mode are:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Mean = (1 + 4 + 0 + 7 + 9)/5 = 21/5 = 4.2. Step 2: Arranged: 0, 1, 4, 7, 9; n = 5 is odd, median = 3rd value = 4. Step 3: Every value occurs once, so there is no mode.

mcqs.q: For the data 148, 145, 160, 157, 156, 160, the correct order is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Mean = 926/6 = 154.33. Step 2: Arranged: 145, 148, 156, 157, 160, 160; median = (1/2)(156 + 157) = 156.5. Step 3: Mode = 160 (occurs twice). So Mode 160 > Median 156.5 > Mean 154.33.

Midpoints: 17, 22, 27, 32, 37. Step 1: Sum(fx) = 153 + 396 + 945 + 544 + 185 = 2223. Step 2: Sum(f) = 84. Step 3: Formula: Mean = Sum(fx)/Sum(f) = 2223/84 = 26.46. (26.64 is the MEDIAN of this distribution.)

mcqs.q: The median of the same grouped marks distribution is:
mcqs.why: Cumulative frequencies: 9, 27, 62, 79, 84; n/2 = 42 lies in class 24.5-29.5. Formula: Median = l + (h/f)(n/2 - c) = 24.5 + (5/35)(42 - 27) = 24.5 + 2.14 = 26.64 marks.

mcqs.q: The mean of the same pocket-money data (by the coding method) is:
Food items: rice 10 kg at Rs. 96/kg, flour 12 kg at Rs. 48, ghee 4 kg at Rs. 190, sugar 3 kg at Rs. 49, mutton 2 kg at Rs. 650. The weighted mean cost per kg is:
options: Rs. 294.40 (the simple mean of the five prices)
mcqs.why: Formula: Weighted mean = Sum(WX)/Sum(W), weights = quantities. Step 1: Sum(WX) = 960 + 576 + 760 + 147 + 1300 = 3743. Step 2: Sum(W) = 31 kg. Step 3: 3743/31 = Rs. 120.74 per kg. The simple mean of prices (1472/5 = 294.40) ignores the quantities, so it is wrong here.

mcqs.q: Ahmad's marks with weights: Urdu 78 (5), English 65 (4), Science 80 (2), Math 90 (3), Islamiyat 85 (2), Computer 72 (4). His weighted mean is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Weighted mean = Sum(WX)/Sum(W). Step 1: Sum(WX) = 390 + 260 + 160 + 270 + 170 + 288 = 1538. Step 2: Sum(W) = 20. Step 3: 1538/20 = 76.9 marks.

mcqs.q: If D = X - 140 with Sum(D) = 500 and n = 10, the mean is:
mcqs.why: Short formula: Mean = A + Sum(D)/n, where A is the value subtracted, 140. Step: Mean = 140 + 500/10 = 140 + 50 = 190.

mcqs.q: Haris (50, 55, 70, 85, 90), Maham (75, 60, 60, 45, 53) and Minal (80, 77, 66, 42, 48) compete for a Rs. 1000 award for the highest average. The winner is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Average = sum of 5 scores / 5. Step: Haris: 350/5 = 70. Maham: 293/5 = 58.6. Minal: 313/5 = 62.6. Haris has the highest average, so Haris gets the award.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 12
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 (i)

Which data takes only some specific values?
(a) continuous data   (b) discrete data   (c) grouped data   (d) ungrouped data
Correct answer: discrete data

Q1 (ii)

The number of times a value occurs in a data is called:
(a) frequency   (b) relative frequency   (c) class limit   (d) class boundaries
Correct answer: frequency

Q1 (iii)

Midpoint is also known as:
(a) mean   (b) median   (c) class limit   (d) class mark
Correct answer: class mark

Q1 (iv)

Frequency polygon is also drawn/constructed by using:
(a) histogram   (b) bar graph   (c) class boundaries   (d) class limit
Correct answer: histogram

Q1 (v)

The difference between the greatest value and the smallest value is called:
(a) class limits   (b) midpoint   (c) relative frequency   (d) range
Correct answer: range

Q1 (vi)

Measure of central tendency is used to find out the ______ of a data set.
(a) class boundaries   (b) cumulative frequency   (c) middle or centre value   (d) frequency
Correct answer: middle or centre value

Q1 (vii)

If the mean of 5, 7, 8, 9 and x is 7.5, what will be the value of x?
(a) 10   (b) 8   (c) 8.5   (d) 5.8
Correct answer: 8.5

Q1 (viii)

Find the mode of the given data: 2, 5, 8, 9, 0, 1, 3, 7 and 10
(a) 5   (b) 7   (c) 0   (d) no mode
Correct answer: no mode

Q1 (ix)

In a data the values (observations) which appears or occurs most often is called:
(a) mean   (b) mode   (c) median   (d) weighted mean
Correct answer: mode

Q1 (x)

Find the median of the given data: 110, 125, 122, 130, 124, 127 and 120
(a) 124   (b) 120   (c) 125   (d) 127
Correct answer: 124

Q2: Define the following

(i) frequency distribution (ii) histogram (unequal class limits) (iii) mean (iv) median

(i) Frequency distribution: A table that shows the data divided into classes or groups together with the number of observations (frequency) falling in each class. It organises raw data into a summarised, easy-to-read form.

(ii) Histogram (unequal class limits): A graph of a frequency distribution made of touching rectangles whose bases are the class boundaries and whose areas are proportional to the class frequencies. When class widths are unequal, the height of each rectangle is the adjusted frequency = frequency / width of the class.

(iii) Mean: The arithmetic average of a set of values, found by dividing the sum of all the values by the number of values: Mean = Sum(x)/n. For grouped data, Mean = Sum(fx)/Sum(f), where x is the midpoint of each class.

(iv) Median: The middle value of the data arranged in ascending or descending order; half the observations lie before it and half after it. For grouped data, Median = l + (h/f)(n/2 - c), where l is the lower class boundary of the median class, h its size, f its frequency and c the cumulative frequency before it.

Q3: Following are the weights of 40 students recorded to the nearest (lbs). (a) Make a frequency table by taking number of classes as 6 (b) Draw histogram (c) Draw a frequency polygon of the given data

Make the table, histogram and polygon.

Data (40 weights in lbs): 138, 164, 150, 132, 144, 125, 149, 157, 146, 158, 140, 147, 136, 148, 152, 144, 168, 126, 138, 176, 163, 119, 154, 165, 146, 173, 142, 147, 135, 153, 140, 135, 161, 145, 135, 142, 150, 156, 145, 128.

(a) Step 1: Range = 176 - 119 = 57. Size of class = 57/6 = 9.5, taken as 10. Frequency table (6 classes):
Class 119-128: f = 4
Class 129-138: f = 7
Class 139-148: f = 13
Class 149-158: f = 9
Class 159-168: f = 5
Class 169-178: f = 2
Total = 40 ✓.

(b) Histogram (in words): Class boundaries: 118.5-128.5, 128.5-138.5, 138.5-148.5, 148.5-158.5, 158.5-168.5, 168.5-178.5. Draw touching rectangles on these intervals with heights 4, 7, 13, 9, 5, 2; the tallest rectangle is over 138.5-148.5.

(c) Frequency polygon (in words): Midpoints are 123.5, 133.5, 143.5, 153.5, 163.5, 173.5. Plot (123.5, 4), (133.5, 7), (143.5, 13), (153.5, 9), (163.5, 5), (173.5, 2), join in order with straight segments and extend the ends to the x-axis.

Q4: From the table given below. Draw a frequency polygon on histogram for the given frequency distribution. Weight (kg): 50-56 (25), 57-59 (32), 60-64 (40), 65-72 (30), 73-75 (15), 76-80 (8)

Draw the frequency polygon on the histogram.

The class widths are unequal, so the polygon is built on the histogram with adjusted frequencies: Formula: Height = f / width (widths measured on class boundaries).

Step 1: Class boundaries and widths: 49.5-56.5 (7), 56.5-59.5 (3), 59.5-64.5 (5), 64.5-72.5 (8), 72.5-75.5 (3), 75.5-80.5 (5).

Step 2: Adjusted heights: 25/7 = 3.57; 32/3 = 10.67; 40/5 = 8; 30/8 = 3.75; 15/3 = 5; 8/5 = 1.6.

Step 3: Histogram (in words): rectangles on the six boundary intervals with heights 3.57, 10.67, 8, 3.75, 5, 1.6 — the narrow class 57-59 gives the tallest rectangle.

Step 4: Frequency polygon: Midpoints: 53, 58, 62, 68.5, 74, 78. Plot (53, 3.57), (58, 10.67), (62, 8), (68.5, 3.75), (74, 5), (78, 1.6) and join in order with straight segments.

Q5: Given below are marks obtained by 45 students in the monthly test of Biology: Marks 20-24 (05), 25-29 (08), 30-34 (12), 35-39 (15), 40-44 (03), 45-49 (02). With reference to the above table find the following: (i) upper class boundary of the 5th class. (ii) lower class boundaries of all the classes. (iii) midpoint of all the classes. (iv) the class interval with the least frequency

Find (i)-(iv).

Classes: 20-24 (05), 25-29 (08), 30-34 (12), 35-39 (15), 40-44 (03), 45-49 (02). Class boundaries are found by subtracting/adding 0.5.

(i) The 5th class is 40-44; its upper class boundary is 44 + 0.5 = 44.5.

(ii) Lower class boundaries of all the classes: 19.5, 24.5, 29.5, 34.5, 39.5, 44.5.

(iii) Midpoints: Formula: Midpoint = (lower limit + upper limit)/2: (20+24)/2 = 22; (25+29)/2 = 27; (30+34)/2 = 32; (35+39)/2 = 37; (40+44)/2 = 42; (45+49)/2 = 47.

(iv) The least frequency is 2, in the class interval 45-49.

Q6: Given below is frequency distribution. Draw frequency polygon and histogram for the distribution. Class limits: 5-9 (1), 10-14 (8), 15-19 (18), 20-24 (11), 25-29 (2), 30-34 (5)

Draw the histogram and frequency polygon.

Step 1: Histogram (in words): Class boundaries: 4.5-9.5, 9.5-14.5, 14.5-19.5, 19.5-24.5, 24.5-29.5, 29.5-34.5. Draw touching rectangles on these intervals with heights equal to the frequencies: 1, 8, 18, 11, 2, 5. The tallest rectangle is over 14.5-19.5.

Step 2: Frequency polygon (in words): Midpoints: 7, 12, 17, 22, 27, 32. Plot the points (7, 1), (12, 8), (17, 18), (22, 11), (27, 2), (32, 5), join them in order with straight line segments, and extend both ends down to the x-axis at midpoints 2 and 37.

Q7: For the following data, find the weighted mean. Chair: quantity 20, cost Rs. 500; Table: 20, Rs. 400; Black board: 10, Rs. 750; Tube light: 25, Rs. 230; Cupboard: 09, Rs. 950

Find the weighted mean.

Quantities are the weights and costs per item are the values. Formula: Weighted mean = Sum(WX)/Sum(W).

Step 1: WX values: Chair: 20 x 500 = 10,000. Table: 20 x 400 = 8,000. Black board: 10 x 750 = 7,500. Tube light: 25 x 230 = 5,750. Cupboard: 9 x 950 = 8,550. Sum(WX) = 39,800.

Step 2: Sum(W) = 20 + 20 + 10 + 25 + 9 = 84.

Step 3: Weighted mean = 39,800/84 = Rs. 473.81 (approx) per item.

Q8: A principal of a school allocates funds of Rs. 50,000 to five different sectors: (i) chairs: Rs. 15,000 (ii) tables: Rs. 12,000 (iii) black boards: Rs. 6,000 (iv) room renovation: Rs. 10,000 (v) gardening: Rs. 7,000. Find the average of funds allocation in each sector of the school

Find the average allocation.

The five allocations are: chairs Rs. 15,000; tables Rs. 12,000; black boards Rs. 6,000; room renovation Rs. 10,000; gardening Rs. 7,000.

Step 1: Check the total: 15,000 + 12,000 + 6,000 + 10,000 + 7,000 = Rs. 50,000 ✓ (the amount allocated).

Step 2: Formula: Average = Total / number of sectors = 50,000/5 = Rs. 10,000.

Hence the average fund allocation in each sector is Rs. 10,000.

Q9: The marks of a student Saad in six tests were 84, 91, 72, 68, 87, 78. Find the arithmetic mean of his marks

Find the mean.

Formula: Mean = Sum of marks / number of tests.

Step 1: Sum = 84 + 91 + 72 + 68 + 87 + 78 = 480.

Step 2: Mean = 480/6 = 80.

Hence the arithmetic mean of Saad's marks is 80.

Q10: Adjoining distribution showed maximum load (in kg) supported by certain ropes. Find the mean load using short method. Max-Load kg: 93-97 (2), 98-102 (5), 103-107 (8), 108-112 (12), 113-117 (6), 118-122 (2)

Find the mean load.

Midpoints x: 95, 100, 105, 110, 115, 120; f: 2, 5, 8, 12, 6, 2; Sum(f) = 35.

Short method: Take A = 110. D = x - A: -15, -10, -5, 0, 5, 10. fD: 2x(-15) = -30; 5x(-10) = -50; 8x(-5) = -40; 12x0 = 0; 6x5 = 30; 2x10 = 20. Sum(fD) = -70.

Formula: Mean = A + Sum(fD)/Sum(f) = 110 + (-70)/35 = 110 - 2 = 108 kg.

Hence the mean maximum load is 108 kg.

Q11: Usman rolled a fair dice eight times. Each time their sum was recorded as 8, 5, 6, 6, 9, 4, 3, 11. Find the median and mode of the sum

Find the median and mode.

Data: 8, 5, 6, 6, 9, 4, 3, 11.

Median: Arrange in ascending order: 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 8, 9, 11. n = 8 is even, so Median = (1/2)(4th + 5th observations) = (1/2)(6 + 6) = 6.

Mode: 6 occurs twice, more than any other sum, so Mode = 6.

Q12: Two partners Mr. Aslam and Mrs. Kalsoom run a company. In the following data the weekly wages (in Rs.) of employees who work in the company are given: Wages (Rs.) 600-700 (3), 700-800 (5), 800-900 (7), 900-1000 (21), 1000-1100 (11)

Find the mean, median and mode of the wages (see Note in the answer about the cut-off instruction line).

Note: In the printed book the instruction line of this question is cut off at the end of the page; the standard quantities asked for such a distribution — mean, median and mode — are all computed here. Flagged in the manifest.

Midpoints x: 650, 750, 850, 950, 1050; f: 3, 5, 7, 21, 11; Sum(f) = 47.

Mean: fx: 1950, 3750, 5950, 19,950, 11,550. Sum(fx) = 43,150. Mean = 43,150/47 = Rs. 918.09 (approx).

Median: Cumulative frequencies: 3, 8, 15, 36, 47. n/2 = 23.5 lies in the class 900-1000. l = 900, h = 100, f = 21, c = 15. Median = 900 + (100/21)(23.5 - 15) = 900 + 40.48 = Rs. 940.48 (approx).

Mode: Modal class 900-1000: fm = 21, f1 = 7, f2 = 11. Mode = 900 + [(21 - 7)/((21 - 7) + (21 - 11))] x 100 = 900 + (14/24) x 100 = 900 + 58.33 = Rs. 958.33 (approx).

mcqs.q: Data that takes only some specific values (like number of heads, 0 to 5) is called:
mcqs.why: Discrete data can take only particular separated values — counts such as the number of heads in 5 tosses (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5). Continuous data (heights, weights) can take any value in a range.

mcqs.q: The number of times a value occurs in data is called its:
mcqs.why: Frequency counts the occurrences of a value or class. (Relative frequency is the frequency divided by the total; class limits and boundaries describe the ends of a class.)

mcqs.q: The midpoint of a class is also known as the:
mcqs.why: Midpoint = (lower limit + upper limit)/2, and it is also called the class mark — the representative value of the class used in mean calculations.

mcqs.q: A frequency polygon can also be constructed by using a:
mcqs.why: Mark the top-centre point of each histogram rectangle (midpoint, frequency) and join the points in order — that gives the frequency polygon on the histogram, as done in Exercises 12.1 Q.5 and Q.8.

mcqs.q: The difference between the greatest value and the smallest value is called the:
mcqs.why: Formula: Range = greatest value - smallest value. It is the first step in deciding class size: Size = Range / number of classes.

mcqs.q: A measure of central tendency is used to find the ______ of a data set.
mcqs.why: Mean, median and mode are measures of central tendency: each gives a single central value that represents the whole data set.

mcqs.q: If the mean of 5, 7, 8, 9 and x is 7.5, then x is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Mean = Sum/n. Step 1: Sum = 5 + 7 + 8 + 9 + x = 29 + x. Step 2: (29 + x)/5 = 7.5 gives 29 + x = 37.5. Step 3: x = 8.5.
Every value in this data occurs exactly once, so no value occurs 'most often' — the data has no mode.

mcqs.q: In data, the value which appears or occurs most often is called the:
mcqs.why: That is the definition of the mode. The mean is the sum divided by the count, and the median is the middle value when the data is arranged in order.
Step 1: Arrange in ascending order: 110, 120, 122, 124, 125, 127, 130. Step 2: n = 7 is odd, so the median is the 4th value = 124.

mcqs.q: For Biology marks 20-24 (05), 25-29 (08), 30-34 (12), 35-39 (15), 40-44 (03), 45-49 (02): the upper class boundary of the 5th class and the least-frequency class are:
mcqs.why: Step 1: The 5th class is 40-44; add half the gap (0.5): upper boundary = 44.5. Step 2: The frequencies are 5, 8, 12, 15, 3, 2 — the smallest is 2, in the class 45-49.

mcqs.q: The midpoints of those Biology classes (20-24 up to 45-49) are:
Saad's marks in six tests are 84, 91, 72, 68, 87, 78. His arithmetic mean is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Mean = Sum/n. Step 1: Sum = 84 + 91 + 72 + 68 + 87 + 78 = 480. Step 2: Mean = 480/6 = 80.

mcqs.q: Max-load data (midpoints 95, 100, 105, 110, 115, 120; f: 2, 5, 8, 12, 6, 2) by the short method with A = 110 gives a mean load of:
Usman recorded dice sums 8, 5, 6, 6, 9, 4, 3, 11. The median and mode are:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Arrange: 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 8, 9, 11; n = 8, median = (1/2)(4th + 5th) = (1/2)(6 + 6) = 6. Step 2: 6 occurs twice, more than any other sum, so mode = 6.

mcqs.q: A principal allocates Rs. 50,000 as 15,000, 12,000, 6,000, 10,000, 7,000 to five sectors. The average allocation per sector is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Average = total / number of sectors. Step 1: Total = 15000 + 12000 + 6000 + 10000 + 7000 = Rs. 50,000. Step 2: Average = 50000/5 = Rs. 10,000 per sector.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: Arshad rolls a dice, with sides labelled L, M, N, O, P, U. What is the probability that the dice lands on consonant?

Find the probability.

Sample space S = {L, M, N, O, P, U}; n(S) = 6.

The vowels are O and U; the consonants are L, M, N, P — 4 favourable outcomes.

Formula: P(consonant) = n(A)/n(S) = 4/6 = 2/3.

Q2: Shazia throws a pair of fair dice. What will be the probability of getting

(i) sum of dots is at least 4 (ii) product of both dots is between 5 to 10 (iii) the difference between both the dots is equal to 4 (iv) number at least 5 on the first dice and the number at least 4 on the second dice

For two fair dice, n(S) = 36. Formula: P(A) = n(A)/n(S).

(i) Sum of dots is at least 4: Use the complement. Sum 2 occurs in 1 way (1,1); sum 3 in 2 ways (1,2), (2,1). So sums less than 4 occur in 3 ways. Favourable = 36 - 3 = 33. P = 33/36 = 11/12.

(ii) Product of both dots is between 5 and 10 (5, 6, 8, 9, 10 are the possible products in this range): product 5: (1,5), (5,1) — 2 ways; product 6: (1,6), (2,3), (3,2), (6,1) — 4 ways; product 8: (2,4), (4,2) — 2 ways; product 9: (3,3) — 1 way; product 10: (2,5), (5,2) — 2 ways. Total = 11 ways. P = 11/36.

(iii) The difference between both the dots is equal to 4: (1,5), (2,6), (5,1), (6,2) — 4 ways. P = 4/36 = 1/9.

(iv) Number at least 5 on the first dice and number at least 4 on the second dice: first dice 5 or 6 (2 ways), second dice 4, 5 or 6 (3 ways): 2 x 3 = 6 ways. P = 6/36 = 1/6.

Q3: One alphabet is selected at random from the word "MATHEMATICS". Find the probability of getting

(i) vowel (ii) consonant (iii) an E (iv) an A (v) not M (vi) not T

The word MATHEMATICS has 11 letters: M, A, T, H, E, M, A, T, I, C, S. Total outcomes n(S) = 11. Vowels: A, A, E, I (4). Consonants: M, M, T, T, H, C, S (7). Formula: P = n(A)/n(S).

(i) Vowel: 4/11.

(ii) Consonant: 7/11.

(iii) An E: there is 1 E: 1/11.

(iv) An A: there are 2 A's: 2/11.

(v) Not M: P = 1 - P(M) = 1 - 2/11 = 9/11.

(vi) Not T: P = 1 - P(T) = 1 - 2/11 = 9/11.

Q4: Aslam rolled a dice. What is the probability of getting the numbers 3 or 4? Also find the probability of not getting the numbers 3 or 4

Find both probabilities.

Sample space S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}; n(S) = 6.

Getting 3 or 4: favourable outcomes {3, 4}, n(A) = 2. Formula: P(3 or 4) = 2/6 = 1/3.

Not getting 3 or 4: Formula: P(A') = 1 - P(A) = 1 - 1/3 = 2/3.

Q5: Abdul Hadi labelled cards from 1 to 30 and put them in a box. He selects a card at random. What is the probability that selected card containing

(i) the number 25 (ii) number between 17 to 22 (iii) number at least 20 (iv) number not 27 and 29 (v) number not between 12 to 15

Total cards n(S) = 30. Formula: P = n(A)/n(S).

(i) The number 25: only one card: 1/30.

(ii) Number between 17 to 22: the cards 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 — 6 cards: 6/30 = 1/5.

(iii) Number at least 20: the cards 20, 21, ..., 30 — 11 cards: 11/30.

(iv) Number not 27 and 29 (i.e. the card is neither 27 nor 29): 30 - 2 = 28 cards: 28/30 = 14/15.

(v) Number not between 12 to 15: the cards 12, 13, 14, 15 are 4 cards, so 30 - 4 = 26 cards: 26/30 = 13/15.

Q6: The probability that Ayesha will pass the examination is 0.85. What will be the probability that Ayesha will not pass the examination?

Find the probability.

Formula: P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

Step 1: P(Ayesha will not pass) = 1 - 0.85 = 0.15.

Hence the probability that Ayesha will not pass the examination is 0.15.

Q7: Taabish tossed a fair coin and rolled a fair dice once. Find the probability of the following events

(i) tail on coin and at least 4 on dice (ii) head on coin and the number 2,3 on dice (iii) head and tail on coin and the number 6 on dice (iv) not tail on coin and the number 5 on dice (v) not head on coin and the number 5 and 2 on dice

A coin (2 outcomes) and a dice (6 outcomes) give n(S) = 2 x 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes: (H,1)...(H,6), (T,1)...(T,6). Formula: P = n(A)/n(S).

(i) Tail on coin and at least 4 on dice: (T,4), (T,5), (T,6) — 3 outcomes: 3/12 = 1/4.

(ii) Head on coin and the number 2 or 3 on dice: (H,2), (H,3) — 2 outcomes: 2/12 = 1/6.

(iii) The number 6 on dice with the coin showing either face: (H,6), (T,6) — 2 outcomes: 2/12 = 1/6. Note: As printed, part (iii) says 'head and tail on coin', which a single coin cannot show at the same time; it is read here as the coin showing head or tail (either face) together with a 6 on the dice. Flagged in the manifest.

(iv) Not tail on coin (i.e. head) and the number 5 on dice: (H,5) — 1 outcome: 1/12.

(v) Not head on coin (i.e. tail) and the number 5 or 2 on dice: (T,5), (T,2) — 2 outcomes: 2/12 = 1/6. Note: As printed, part (v) says 'the number 5 and 2 on dice'; a single dice shows only one number, so it is read as 5 or 2. Flagged in the manifest.

Q8: A card is selected at random from a well shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. What will be the probability of selecting

(i) a queen (ii) neither a queen nor a jack

Total cards n(S) = 52. There are 4 queens and 4 jacks. Formula: P = n(A)/n(S).

(i) A queen: 4/52 = 1/13.

(ii) Neither a queen nor a jack: favourable cards = 52 - 4 - 4 = 44. P = 44/52 = 11/13.

Q9: A card is chosen at random from a pack of 52 playing cards. Find the probability of getting

(i) a jack (ii) no diamond

Total cards n(S) = 52. There are 4 jacks and 13 diamonds. Formula: P = n(A)/n(S).

(i) A jack: 4/52 = 1/13.

(ii) No diamond: Formula: P = 1 - P(diamond) = 1 - 13/52 = 39/52 = 3/4.

mcqs.q: A dice has faces labelled L, M, N, O, P, U. The probability that it lands on a consonant is:
mcqs.why: Sample space S = {L, M, N, O, P, U}, n(S) = 6. The vowels are O and U; the consonants are L, M, N, P — 4 favourable outcomes. Formula: P = n(A)/n(S) = 4/6 = 2/3.

mcqs.q: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that the sum of dots is at least 4 is:
mcqs.why: Use the complement. Sums less than 4: sum 2 in 1 way (1,1) and sum 3 in 2 ways (1,2), (2,1) — 3 ways out of 36. Favourable = 36 - 3 = 33. Formula: P = 33/36 = 11/12.

mcqs.q: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that the difference between the dots is exactly 4 is:
mcqs.why: The favourable pairs are (1,5), (2,6), (5,1), (6,2) — 4 outcomes out of n(S) = 36. Formula: P = 4/36 = 1/9.

mcqs.q: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability of at least 5 on the first dice and at least 4 on the second is:
mcqs.why: First dice 5 or 6: 2 ways. Second dice 4, 5 or 6: 3 ways. Total favourable = 2 x 3 = 6 out of 36. Formula: P = 6/36 = 1/6.

mcqs.q: One letter is chosen at random from the word MATHEMATICS (11 letters). The probability of a vowel is:
mcqs.why: The letters are M, A, T, H, E, M, A, T, I, C, S. The vowels are A, A, E, I — 4 of the 11 letters. Formula: P = 4/11. (Consonants are the other 7, giving 7/11.)

mcqs.q: From the same word, the probability of NOT getting M is:
mcqs.why: There are 2 M's, so P(M) = 2/11. Formula: P(not M) = 1 - P(M) = 1 - 2/11 = 9/11.

mcqs.q: The probability that Ayesha passes an examination is 0.85. The probability that she will NOT pass is:
mcqs.why: Formula: P(not A) = 1 - P(A). Step: 1 - 0.85 = 0.15.

mcqs.q: A card is drawn from a pack of 52. The probability of selecting neither a queen nor a jack is:
mcqs.why: There are 4 queens and 4 jacks. Favourable cards = 52 - 4 - 4 = 44. Formula: P = 44/52 = 11/13.

mcqs.q: A card is drawn from a pack of 52. The probability of getting no diamond is:
mcqs.why: There are 13 diamonds, so P(diamond) = 13/52 = 1/4. Formula: P(no diamond) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4 (equivalently 39/52).

mcqs.q: Cards numbered 1 to 30 are in a box. The probability that a card drawn at random shows a number at least 20 is:
mcqs.why: The numbers at least 20 are 20, 21, ..., 30 — that is 11 cards out of 30. Formula: P = 11/30.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1: A researcher collected data on number of deaths from Horse-Kicks in Russian Army corps over years. No. of death: 0 (60), 1 (50), 2 (87), 3 (40), 4 (32), 5 (15), 6 (10). Find the relative frequency of the given data

Find the relative frequencies.

Formula: Relative frequency = (frequency of the specific value) / (total frequency).

Step 1: Total frequency N = 60 + 50 + 87 + 40 + 32 + 15 + 10 = 294.

Step 2: Relative frequencies: 0 deaths: 60/294 = 0.204; 1 death: 50/294 = 0.170; 2 deaths: 87/294 = 0.296; 3 deaths: 40/294 = 0.136; 4 deaths: 32/294 = 0.109; 5 deaths: 15/294 = 0.051; 6 deaths: 10/294 = 0.034.

(Check: the relative frequencies add to 1.000 approx.)

Q2: The frequency of defective products in 750 samples are shown in the following table. Find the relative frequency for the given table. No. of defectives per sample: 0 (120), 1 (140), 2 (94), 3 (85), 4 (105), 5 (50), 6 (40), 7 (66), 8 (50)

Find the relative frequencies.

Formula: Relative frequency = (number of samples with the given defectives) / (total samples). Total samples = 750 (check: 120 + 140 + 94 + 85 + 105 + 50 + 40 + 66 + 50 = 750 ✓).

Relative frequencies: 0 defectives: 120/750 = 0.16; 1: 140/750 = 0.187; 2: 94/750 = 0.125; 3: 85/750 = 0.113; 4: 105/750 = 0.14; 5: 50/750 = 0.067; 6: 40/750 = 0.053; 7: 66/750 = 0.088; 8: 50/750 = 0.067.

(Check: they add to 1.000 approx.)

Q3: A quiz competition on general knowledge is conducted. The number of corrected answers out of 5 questions for 100 sets of questions is given below. X: 0 (10), 1 (23), 2 (15), 3 (25), 4 (18), 5 (9). Find the relative frequencies for the given data

Find the relative frequencies.

Formula: Relative frequency = f / N. Total N = 10 + 23 + 15 + 25 + 18 + 9 = 100.

Relative frequencies: X = 0: 10/100 = 0.10; X = 1: 23/100 = 0.23; X = 2: 15/100 = 0.15; X = 3: 25/100 = 0.25; X = 4: 18/100 = 0.18; X = 5: 9/100 = 0.09.

(Check: 0.10 + 0.23 + 0.15 + 0.25 + 0.18 + 0.09 = 1.00 ✓.)

Q4: A survey was conducted from the 108 students of a class and asked about their favourite food. The responses are as under: Biryani 40, Fresh Juice 07, Chicken 21, Bar. B.Q 15, Sweets 25

(i) how many percentages of students like biryani? (ii) how many percentages of students like chicken? (iii) which food is the least like by the students? (iv) which food is the most prefer by the students?

Total students = 40 + 7 + 21 + 15 + 25 = 108. Percentage = relative frequency x 100.

(i) Like biryani: (40/108) x 100 = 37.04% (approx).

(ii) Like chicken: (21/108) x 100 = 19.44% (approx).

(iii) The least liked food is Fresh Juice — only 7 students chose it (relative frequency 7/108 = 0.065, about 6.5%).

(iv) The most preferred food is Biryani — 40 students chose it, the highest frequency.

Q5: In 500 trials of a thrown of two dice, what is expected frequency that the sum will be greater than 8?

Find the expected frequency.

Step 1: For two dice, sums greater than 8 are 9, 10, 11, 12, occurring in 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 ways out of 36. Formula: P(sum > 8) = 10/36 = 5/18.

Step 2: Formula: Expected frequency = N x P = 500 x (5/18) = 2500/18 = 138.89.

Hence in 500 throws the sum is expected to be greater than 8 about 139 times.

Q6: What is the expectation of a person who is to get Rs. 120 if he obtains at least 2 heads in single toss of three coins?

Find the expectation.

Three coins tossed together give 8 equally likely outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.

Step 1: At least 2 heads occurs in HHH, HHT, HTH, THH — 4 outcomes. P(win) = 4/8 = 1/2.

Step 2: Formula: Expectation = amount to be received x probability of the event = 120 x (1/2) = Rs. 60.

Hence the person's expectation is Rs. 60.

Q7: Find the expected frequencies of the given data if the experiment is repeated 200 times. x: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 with P(x): 0.11, 0.21, 0.17, 0.18, 0.09, 0.17, 0.07

Find the expected frequencies.

Formula: Expected frequency = N x P(x), with N = 200.

x = 0: 200 x 0.11 = 22
x = 1: 200 x 0.21 = 42
x = 2: 200 x 0.17 = 34
x = 3: 200 x 0.18 = 36
x = 4: 200 x 0.09 = 18
x = 5: 200 x 0.17 = 34
x = 6: 200 x 0.07 = 14

(Check: 22 + 42 + 34 + 36 + 18 + 34 + 14 = 200 ✓, and the given probabilities add to 1.00.)

Q8: The probability of getting 5 sixes while tossing six dice is 2/5, the dice is rolled 200 times. How many times would you expect it to show 5 sixes?

Find the expected number of times.

Formula: Expected frequency = N x P.

Step 1: Expected number of times = 200 x (2/5) = 400/5 = 80.

Hence you would expect it to show 5 sixes about 80 times in 200 rolls.

mcqs.q: Deaths data: frequencies 60, 50, 87, 40, 32, 15, 10 for 0 to 6 deaths (total 294). The relative frequency of 2 deaths is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Relative frequency = f / total frequency. Step: For 2 deaths, f = 87 and total = 294, so 87/294 = 0.296. (0.204 is the relative frequency of 0 deaths.)

mcqs.q: Relative frequencies of all values in a data set always add up to:
mcqs.why: Each relative frequency is f/N, and the frequencies add to N, so the relative frequencies add to N/N = 1. In the deaths data: 0.204 + 0.170 + 0.296 + 0.136 + 0.109 + 0.051 + 0.034 = 1.000.

mcqs.q: In a survey of 108 students, 40 like biryani. The percentage who like biryani is:
mcqs.why: Percentage = relative frequency x 100. Step: (40/108) x 100 = 0.3704 x 100 = 37.04% approximately. (19.44% is the percentage for chicken, 21 students.)

mcqs.q: In 500 throws of two dice, the expected frequency of a sum greater than 8 is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Sums 9, 10, 11, 12 occur in 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 ways out of 36, so P = 10/36 = 5/18. Step 2: Formula: Expected frequency = N x P = 500 x 5/18 = 138.89, about 139 times.

mcqs.q: A person receives Rs. 120 if he gets at least 2 heads in one toss of three coins. His expectation is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Three coins give 8 outcomes; at least 2 heads occurs in HHH, HHT, HTH, THH — 4 outcomes, so P = 4/8 = 1/2. Step 2: Formula: Expectation = amount x probability = 120 x 1/2 = Rs. 60.

mcqs.q: With N = 200 and P(x = 4) = 0.09, the expected frequency of x = 4 is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Expected frequency = N x P(x). Step: 200 x 0.09 = 18. (All seven expected frequencies 22, 42, 34, 36, 18, 34, 14 add to 200, as they must.)

mcqs.q: Using the probability given in the book, P(5 sixes in six dice) = 2/5. In 200 rolls, the expected number of times is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Expected frequency = N x P. Step: 200 x (2/5) = 400/5 = 80 times.

mcqs.q: In the quiz data (100 sets; correct answers 0-5 with f: 10, 23, 15, 25, 18, 9), the relative frequency of exactly 3 correct answers is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Relative frequency = f/N. Step: f = 25 and N = 100, so 25/100 = 0.25 — the most frequent score in this data.

mcqs.q: In the food survey, the LEAST liked food was:
mcqs.why: Frequencies: Biryani 40, Sweets 25, Chicken 21, Bar B.Q 15, Fresh Juice 7. The smallest frequency, 7, belongs to Fresh Juice (relative frequency 7/108 = 0.065, about 6.5%).

mcqs.q: Defective products: in 750 samples, 120 samples have 0 defectives. The relative frequency of 0 defectives is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Relative frequency = f / total. Step: 120/750 = 0.16. (0.187 belongs to 1 defective, 140/750, and 0.125 to 2 defectives.)

lessons.title: Review Exercise 13
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 (i)

Each element of the sample space is called:
(a) event   (b) experiment   (c) sample point   (d) outcomes
Correct answer: sample point

Q1 (ii)

An outcome which represents how many times we expect the things to be happened is called:
(a) outcomes   (b) favourable outcome   (c) sample space   (d) sample point
Correct answer: favourable outcome

Q1 (iii)

Which one tells us how often a specific event occurs relative to the total number of frequency event or trials?
(a) expected frequency   (b) sum of relative frequency   (c) relative frequency   (d) frequency
Correct answer: relative frequency

Q1 (iv)

Estimated probability of an event occurring is also known as:
(a) relative frequency   (b) expected frequency   (c) class boundaries   (d) sum of expected frequency
Correct answer: relative frequency

Q1 (v)

The sum of all expected frequencies is equal to the fixed number of:
(a) trials   (b) relative frequencies   (c) outcomes   (d) events
Correct answer: trials

Q1 (vi)

The chance of occurrence of a particular event is called:
(a) sample space   (b) estimated probability   (c) probability   (d) expected frequency
Correct answer: probability

Q1 (vii)

An event which will probably occur. It has greater chance to occur is called:
(a) equally likely event   (b) likely event   (c) unlikely event   (d) certain event
Correct answer: likely event

Q1 (viii)

Find out the total number of possible sample space when 4 dice are rolled:
(a) 6^2   (b) 6^3   (c) 6^4   (d) 6^6
Correct answer: 6^4

Q1 (ix)

While rolling a pair of dice, what will be the probability of double 2?
(a) 1/6   (b) 1/3   (c) 5/6   (d) 1/36
Correct answer: 1/36

Q1 (x)

A card is chosen from a pack of 52 playing cards, find the probability of getting no jack and king:
(a) 2/13   (b) 11/13   (c) 2/52   (d) 11/52
Correct answer: 11/13

Q2: Define the following

(i) relative frequency (ii) expected frequency

(i) Relative frequency: The ratio of the frequency of a specific event to the total frequency (total number of trials): Relative frequency = (frequency of the specific event) / (total frequency). It is used as an estimate of the probability of the event.

(ii) Expected frequency: The number of times an event is expected to occur in a given number of trials, found from its probability: Expected frequency = (total number of trials) x (probability of the event) = N x P(A). The sum of all expected frequencies equals the total number of trials.

Q3: An urn contains 10 red balls, 5 green balls and 8 blue balls. Find the probability of selecting at random

(i) a green ball (ii) a red ball (iii) a blue ball (iv) not a red ball (v) not a green ball

Total balls n(S) = 10 + 5 + 8 = 23. Formula: P = n(A)/n(S).

(i) A green ball: 5/23.

(ii) A red ball: 10/23.

(iii) A blue ball: 8/23.

(iv) Not a red ball: 1 - 10/23 = 13/23.

(v) Not a green ball: 1 - 5/23 = 18/23.

Q4: Three coins are tossed together. What is the probability of getting

(i) exactly three heads (ii) at least two tails (iii) not at least two heads (iv) not exactly two heads

Sample space for three coins: S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT}; n(S) = 8. Formula: P = n(A)/n(S).

(i) Exactly three heads: only HHH — 1 outcome: 1/8.

(ii) At least two tails: HTT, THT, TTH, TTT — 4 outcomes: 4/8 = 1/2.

(iii) Not at least two heads: at least two heads occurs in HHH, HHT, HTH, THH (4 outcomes, probability 1/2), so P(not) = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2.

(iv) Not exactly two heads: exactly two heads occurs in HHT, HTH, THH (3 outcomes, probability 3/8), so P(not) = 1 - 3/8 = 5/8.

Q5: A card is drawn from a well shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. What will be the probability of getting

(i) king or jack of red colour (ii) not "2" of club and spade

Total cards n(S) = 52. Formula: P = n(A)/n(S).

(i) King or jack of red colour: Red cards are hearts and diamonds. Red kings = 2, red jacks = 2, total favourable = 4. P = 4/52 = 1/13.

(ii) Not "2" of club and spade: The 2 of clubs and the 2 of spades are 2 cards; all other 50 cards are favourable. P = 50/52 = 25/26.

Q6: Six coins are tossed 600 times. The number of occurrence of tails are recorded and shown in the table given below: No. of tails 0 (110), 1 (90), 2 (105), 3 (80), 4 (76), 5 (123), 6 (16). Find the relative frequency of given table

Find the relative frequencies.

Formula: Relative frequency = f / N. Total frequency N = 110 + 90 + 105 + 80 + 76 + 123 + 16 = 600 ✓ (the coins were tossed 600 times).

Relative frequencies: 0 tails: 110/600 = 0.183; 1 tail: 90/600 = 0.15; 2 tails: 105/600 = 0.175; 3 tails: 80/600 = 0.133; 4 tails: 76/600 = 0.127; 5 tails: 123/600 = 0.205; 6 tails: 16/600 = 0.027.

(Check: they add to 1.000 approx.)

Q7: From a lot containing 25 items, 8 items are defective. Find the relative frequency of non-defective items, also find the expected frequency of non-defective items

Find both frequencies.

Step 1: Non-defective items = 25 - 8 = 17.

Step 2: Formula: Relative frequency of non-defective items = 17/25 = 0.68. This is also the estimated probability that an item is non-defective.

Step 3: Formula: Expected frequency = N x P. For a lot of the same size (N = 25): 25 x 0.68 = 17 items. In general, in any N items the expected number of non-defective items is 0.68 x N (for example, 68 out of every 100 items).

Note: The book does not state a separate number of trials for the expected frequency, so it is computed for a lot of 25, with the general rule given. Flagged in the manifest.

mcqs.q: Each element of the sample space is called a:
mcqs.why: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes; each single element of it is a sample point. An event is a subset of the sample space, and the experiment is the action performed.

mcqs.q: Which one tells us how often a specific event occurs relative to the total frequency or number of trials?
mcqs.why: Relative frequency = (frequency of the specific event)/(total frequency). It measures the share of trials in which the event occurred, unlike the plain frequency, which is just a count.

mcqs.q: The estimated probability of an event occurring is also known as its:
mcqs.why: When probability is estimated from observed data, the estimate used is the relative frequency of the event in the trials performed.

mcqs.q: The sum of all expected frequencies is equal to the fixed number of:
mcqs.why: Expected frequencies are N x P for each outcome; since the probabilities add to 1, the expected frequencies add to N x 1 = N, the total number of trials (check in Exercise 13.2 Q.7: they add to 200).

mcqs.q: The chance of occurrence of a particular event is called its:
mcqs.why: Probability is the measure of the chance that an event will occur: P(A) = n(A)/n(S) for equally likely outcomes, a number between 0 and 1.

mcqs.q: An event which will probably occur — it has a greater chance to occur — is called a:
mcqs.why: A likely event has probability greater than 1/2 (more likely to happen than not). A certain event has probability exactly 1, and equally likely outcomes share the same probability.

mcqs.q: The total number of possible outcomes (size of the sample space) when 4 dice are rolled is:
mcqs.why: Each dice has 6 outcomes and the dice are independent, so the counts multiply: 6 x 6 x 6 x 6 = 6^4 = 1296 sample points.

mcqs.q: While rolling a pair of dice, the probability of double 2 (two 2's) is:
mcqs.why: Only one outcome, (2,2), gives double 2, out of n(S) = 36 equally likely pairs. Formula: P = 1/36.

mcqs.q: A card is chosen from a pack of 52. The probability of getting no jack and no king is:
mcqs.why: There are 4 jacks and 4 kings, so favourable cards = 52 - 8 = 44. Formula: P = 44/52 = 11/13.

mcqs.q: An urn contains 10 red, 5 green and 8 blue balls. The probability of NOT selecting a red ball is:
mcqs.why: Total balls = 10 + 5 + 8 = 23. P(red) = 10/23. Formula: P(not red) = 1 - 10/23 = 13/23. (18/23 is P(not green).)

mcqs.q: Three coins are tossed together. The probability of NOT getting exactly two heads is:
mcqs.why: Exactly two heads occurs in HHT, HTH, THH — 3 of the 8 outcomes, so P = 3/8. Formula: P(not exactly two heads) = 1 - 3/8 = 5/8.

mcqs.q: A card is drawn from a pack of 52. The probability of a king or jack of red colour is:
mcqs.why: Red cards are hearts and diamonds: red kings = 2 and red jacks = 2, total 4 favourable cards. Formula: P = 4/52 = 1/13.

mcqs.q: Relative frequency is defined as:
options: the total frequency divided by the number of classes
probability multiplied by the amount won
the frequency of a specific event divided by the total frequency
mcqs.why: Definition: Relative frequency = (frequency of the specific event)/(total frequency). It is the standard estimate of probability from experimental data (Review Q.2).

mcqs.q: From a lot of 25 items, 8 are defective. The relative frequency of non-defective items is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Non-defective items = 25 - 8 = 17. Step 2: Formula: Relative frequency = 17/25 = 0.68. This is also the expected proportion of non-defective items in any similar lot.

mcqs.q: Three coins are tossed together. The probability of at least two tails is:
mcqs.why: At least two tails occurs in HTT, THT, TTH, TTT — 4 of the 8 equally likely outcomes. Formula: P = 4/8 = 1/2.
